title: Lungs, gills, air tubes and hearts: how different animal bodies bring oxygen to their cells

summary.text: A litre of air holds about 26 times as much oxygen as a litre of pond water. So why does a fish die in air, with so much oxygen all round? And why can you never breathe out all the air in your lungs? In this lesson you will watch a paintbrush to see what air does to a gill. You will run the Half-Breath Test with two tumblers to find how many breaths it takes to change the air in a lung. You will also compare the hearts of a fish, a frog and a human, and meet animals whose blood is not shut inside tubes.
summary.art: A girl holding a wet paintbrush over a tumbler of water, with two tumblers of brown and clear water on the table and a notebook sketch of a fish and a pair of lungs.

intro.hook: Air has far more oxygen in it than water has. A fish lifted out of a pond is surrounded by oxygen. So why does the fish suffocate?
intro.text: Every cell of every animal needs oxygen, and every animal has to bring that oxygen in from outside. A fish takes oxygen from water with gills. You take it from air with lungs. A grasshopper takes air in through small holes along the sides of the body, and the blood plays almost no part. These are different answers to one problem. In this lesson you will test a model gill and a model lung with your own hands. Then you will follow the oxygen into the blood and round the body, in your own body and in the bodies of other animals.
intro.art: A split picture: a rohu fish under water with red gills showing behind an open gill cover, and the same kind of fish lying on a wet banana leaf with a large question mark above.

outcomes: I can trace the path of air through the respiratory system and of blood through the circulatory system, and say where the two meet.
I can explain why lungs never empty, and why one breath changes only part of the air inside them.
I can explain how gills take oxygen from water, and why gills stop working in air.
I can explain why water and blood flowing in opposite directions pass on more oxygen than flowing the same way.
I can compare the hearts of a fish, a frog and a human, and say why a second pump helps.
I can say what open and closed circulatory systems are, and name animals with each.
I can describe how insects, frogs and birds get oxygen, and explain why blood does not always carry it.
I can plan a fair test with a model, and say what the model shows and what it leaves out.

terms.meaning: The organs that bring oxygen into a body from outside and send carbon dioxide out. In you, these are the nose, the windpipe, the lungs and the muscles that move air.
terms.example: A fish's respiratory system is the mouth, the gills and the gill covers.
terms.art: An outline of a child's chest showing the nose, windpipe and two lungs coloured in.

terms.meaning: The heart, the blood and the tubes that blood moves through. It carries oxygen, food, waste and warmth round the body.
terms.example: Your circulatory system carries oxygen from your lungs to your toes in under a minute.
terms.art: An outline of a child's body with the heart in the chest and red and blue tubes running to the head, hands and feet.

terms.meaning: The spreading of particles from a place where there are many of them to a place where there are few. It happens by itself, because the particles never stop moving.
terms.example: Oxygen diffuses from the air in your lungs into your blood, because the blood arriving there holds less oxygen.
terms.art: Many dots crowded on the left of a thin wall and a few on the right, with small arrows pointing from left to right.

terms.meaning: The voice box, at the top of the trachea. Air passes through it, and the vocal cords inside it make sound.
terms.example: When you hum, you can feel your larynx buzz if you touch your throat.
terms.art: A side view of a child's throat with the larynx marked just above the trachea.

terms.meaning: The tube that carries air from your throat down to your lungs. Rings of cartilage hold it open.
terms.example: You can feel the bumpy rings of your trachea at the front of your neck.
terms.art: A child's neck from the front with a ringed tube drawn inside it.

terms.meaning: The two tubes that the trachea splits into, one for each lung. Inside the lung they branch again and again into smaller tubes.
terms.example: The bronchi branch about 23 times before they reach the air sacs.
terms.art: An upside-down tree shape of branching tubes inside the outline of two lungs.

terms.meaning: One of the tiny air sacs at the ends of the smallest tubes in a lung. Oxygen passes through its thin wall into the blood. The plural is alveoli.
terms.example: An adult's two lungs hold about 480 million alveoli.
terms.art: A bunch of tiny round sacs like grapes, wrapped in a net of fine red and blue tubes.

terms.meaning: Flow that goes in and then out again by the same path, like the tide on a beach. Air in your lungs moves this way.
terms.example: Your breath is tidal. Water over a fish's gills is not. It goes in at the mouth and out at the gill covers.
terms.art: A lung with one arrow going in and one arrow coming out through the same tube.

terms.meaning: The air that stays in your lungs even after you breathe out as hard as you can. Doctors call the amount the residual volume.
terms.example: An adult has about 1.2 litres of residual air.
terms.art: A pair of lungs after a big breath out, still partly filled with a pale blue colour.

terms.meaning: The air in your nose, trachea and bronchi. It moves in and out with each breath, but it never reaches the alveoli, so it gives no oxygen to the blood.
terms.example: In an adult, about 150 millilitres of each breath only fills the dead space.
terms.art: A windpipe and its first branches shaded grey, with the air sacs beyond them left white.

terms.meaning: A blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart. It has thick, stretchy walls. The beat you feel at your wrist is an artery swelling.
terms.example: The aorta is the biggest artery. It carries blood from the left ventricle to the whole body.
terms.art: A thick red tube leaving the heart, with a pulse beat drawn at a wrist.

terms.meaning: A blood vessel that carries blood back to the heart. It has thin walls and small one-way valves.
terms.example: The blue-green lines on the back of your hand are veins.
terms.art: A hand with veins showing on the back, and a small circle showing a valve inside one.

terms.meaning: An organ that takes oxygen out of water. It is made of very many thin plates full of blood, and water flows between the plates.
terms.example: The red, feathery parts under a fish's gill cover are the gills.
terms.art: A fish with the gill cover lifted to show four red arches, each with a fringe of fine red threads.

terms.meaning: One of the fine red threads of a gill. Each filament carries rows of even smaller plates, called lamellae, where the oxygen is taken up.
terms.example: The gills of one fish have hundreds of filaments, and each filament has many lamellae.
terms.art: One red thread shown large, with rows of tiny flat plates standing along both sides of it.

terms.meaning: The hard flap that covers the gills of a bony fish. It opens and closes to help pump water over the gills.
terms.example: When a fish in a tank seems to be chewing, you are watching the operculum open and close.
terms.art: The side of a fish's head with the curved gill cover slightly open and an arrow of water coming out behind it.

terms.meaning: An arrangement in which two liquids flow past each other in opposite directions, with a thin wall between them. It lets one liquid pass on most of what it carries to the other. Scientists also call it countercurrent exchange.
terms.example: In a gill, blood flows forward while water flows backward, and the blood collects most of the oxygen.
terms.art: Two long arrows side by side pointing in opposite directions, one blue and one red, with small arrows crossing from blue to red all along.

terms.meaning: A chamber of the heart that receives blood coming in. The plural is atria.
terms.example: Your heart has two atria, a right one and a left one.
terms.art: A simple heart with the two upper chambers coloured and arrows of blood flowing into them.

terms.meaning: A chamber of the heart with a thick wall of muscle. It pumps blood out of the heart.
terms.example: Your left ventricle pumps blood to your whole body.
terms.art: A simple heart with the two lower chambers coloured, the left one drawn with a much thicker wall.

terms.meaning: A plan in which blood passes through the heart once on each trip round the body. The heart pumps it to the gills, and it goes straight on to the body.
terms.example: A fish has single circulation.
terms.art: One loop: heart, then gills, then body, then back to the heart.

terms.meaning: A plan in which blood passes through the heart twice on each trip. One loop goes to the lungs and back. The other goes to the body and back.
terms.example: Humans, crows and crocodiles have double circulation.
terms.art: A figure of eight with the heart at the crossing, a small loop to the lungs above and a large loop to the body below.

terms.meaning: A system in which the blood stays inside tubes all the way round. The blood never touches the cells directly.
terms.example: Humans, fish, earthworms and octopuses have closed circulatory systems.
terms.art: A ring of tubes with a heart in it and red liquid only inside the tubes.

terms.meaning: A system in which the heart pumps the blood out of short tubes into the spaces of the body. There the liquid washes round the organs before it drifts back to the heart.
terms.example: Grasshoppers, cockroaches, crabs and snails have open circulatory systems.
terms.art: A grasshopper cut open from the side, with a tube heart along the back and pale liquid filling the space round the organs.

terms.meaning: The liquid in an open circulatory system. It does the work of blood and of the liquid round the cells, because in these animals the two are one liquid.
terms.example: The pale liquid that comes out when a cockroach is crushed is haemolymph.
terms.art: A drop of pale greenish liquid beside a small drawing of a cockroach.

terms.meaning: The branching tubes that carry air through the body of an insect. The finest branches end right beside the cells.
terms.example: A grasshopper's tracheae carry air straight to the flight muscles.
terms.art: The outline of a grasshopper with silver branching tubes spreading through the whole body.

terms.meaning: One of the small openings along the sides of an insect's body. Air goes in and out of the tracheae through the spiracles, and many insects can shut them.
terms.example: On a large caterpillar you can see the spiracles as a row of dots, one on each side of most segments.
terms.art: The side of a green caterpillar with a row of small oval dots, one dot ringed and labelled.

terms.meaning: A protein that carries oxygen in the blood of octopuses, crabs, snails and many other animals. It holds copper where our haemoglobin holds iron, and it turns blue when it carries oxygen.
terms.example: An octopus has blue blood because of haemocyanin.
terms.art: A drop of blue liquid beside an octopus, and a drop of red liquid beside a child's finger.

terms.meaning: The watery liquid that leaks out of your capillaries and is collected by a second set of thin tubes. These tubes return it to the blood near the heart.
terms.example: About 3 litres of lymph go back into an adult's blood every day.
terms.art: A capillary with small drops leaking out between cells, and a thin pale tube beside it collecting the drops.

terms.meaning: A heart attack happens when an artery that feeds the heart muscle is blocked, so part of the muscle gets no oxygen. It needs a doctor at once.
terms.example: A grandfather has a heavy chest, sweating and pain spreading to his left arm. His family takes him to hospital straight away.
terms.art: A man holding his chest, with a narrowed artery shown in a small circle beside him.

explanations.definition: The respiratory system brings oxygen from outside to a thin, wet surface. The circulatory system carries that oxygen from the surface to the cells, and brings carbon dioxide back.
explanations.description: Your cells use oxygen to get energy out of food, and they make carbon dioxide as they do it. Most of your cells are deep inside you, far from the air. So two jobs have to be done. Air must be brought close to the blood, and blood must be brought close to every cell. The first job belongs to the respiratory system and the second to the circulatory system. They meet in the lungs, where air and blood are less than a thousandth of a millimetre apart. Not every animal splits the work this way. An insect's air tubes do both jobs, and a flatworm is so thin that the animal needs neither system. Plants need oxygen too, but they have no lungs or blood. Air reaches every leaf and root through tiny pores, and the gases spread in by diffusion. A tulsi plant on a balcony takes in oxygen and gives out carbon dioxide all day and all night, just as you do. In sunlight, its green leaves also make food. While they do that, they give out more oxygen than the plant uses. Air is a mix of gases, and about one fifth of it is oxygen.
examples: In you, air meets blood in about 480 million alveoli.
In a fish, water meets blood on the plates of the gills.
A flatworm is as thin as paper. Oxygen spreads in through the skin and reaches every cell without lungs, gills or blood.
A tulsi plant in the dark takes in oxygen and gives out carbon dioxide, like you.
explanations.art: A child's chest with the lungs drawn in blue and the heart and blood vessels in red, and a small circle zooming in on the place where an air sac touches a capillary.

explanations.concept: The path of air, from nose to alveoli
explanations.definition: Air goes in through the nose, down the trachea, into the two bronchi, through smaller and smaller branches, and ends in the alveoli.
explanations.description: The nose warms the air and makes it damp. Sticky mucus on the walls of the tubes traps dust. Tiny hairs called cilia sweep that mucus up towards the throat all day. The tubes branch about 23 times, which is why the inside of a lung looks like an upside-down tree. Each alveolus is wrapped in capillaries, the thinnest blood vessels. The wall between air and blood is far thinner than a hair. Oxygen crosses this wall by diffusion. It moves from the air, where there is more oxygen, into the blood, where there is less. Carbon dioxide crosses the other way for the same reason. No part of the lung pushes the oxygen across. Before the mucus, short stiff hairs just inside the nose catch the bigger bits of dust. After the nose, air goes down the throat and through the larynx, or voice box, at the top of the trachea. Your vocal cords are inside the larynx, and they make sound when air flows past them.
examples: Breathing through your nose on a cold morning in Ooty feels gentler than breathing through your mouth, because the nose warms the air first.
When you cough up mucus, you are clearing dust that the cilia have swept up.
Spread flat, the alveoli of an adult would cover most of a badminton court.
When you hum, you can feel the buzz of your larynx with your fingers on your throat.
explanations.art: The airways as an upside-down tree, with a magnified circle showing one air sac, its thin wall and a capillary with red blood cells in single file.

explanations.concept: Tidal flow: your lungs never empty
explanations.definition: Air moves in and out of your lungs by the same path. Each breath changes only part of the air in the lungs, and some air always stays behind.
explanations.description: Your lungs are bags with one opening. When you breathe out quietly, an adult's lungs still hold about 2 litres or more of air. The next breath brings in about half a litre. About 150 millilitres of that only fills the nose, trachea and bronchi, so about 350 millilitres of new air reaches the alveoli. There it mixes with the air that stayed behind. So one quiet breath changes roughly one seventh of the air deep in an adult's lungs. This is why the air in your alveoli has less oxygen than room air. Room air is about 21 parts oxygen in 100. The air you breathe out still has about 16 parts in 100. The mixing has a good side. The blood meets a steady mixture, so the oxygen in your blood hardly changes between one breath and the next.
examples: After you breathe out as hard as you can, about a litre of air is still in an adult's lungs. Nobody can push it out.
Mouth-to-mouth rescue breathing works because breathed-out air still holds most of its oxygen.
When you pant after a race, you take bigger and faster breaths, so more of the old air is changed each time.
explanations.art: A pair of lungs drawn three times: after a quiet breath out, mostly full of pale blue; after a breath in, with a small band of fresh colour added at the top; and after mixing, an even colour slightly fresher than before.

explanations.concept: The path of blood: two loops at two pressures
explanations.definition: In double circulation, the right side of the heart pumps blood through the lungs at low pressure. The left side pumps the same blood through the rest of the body at high pressure.
explanations.description: Blood that has given up oxygen comes back from the body into the right atrium and then the right ventricle. The right ventricle pumps it to the lungs. It comes back, full of oxygen, to the left atrium and then the left ventricle. The left ventricle pumps it to the body. Doctors measure blood pressure in millimetres of mercury. In a resting adult, the left ventricle pushes with about 120 of these units at each beat. The right ventricle pushes with only about 25. The lungs need the gentle push, because their capillaries have very thin walls. The body needs the strong push, because the blood has to reach the brain above the heart and the toes far below.
examples: The wall of your left ventricle is much thicker than the wall of your right ventricle, because it pushes much harder.
A giraffe's heart must push blood about 2 metres up to the brain, so a giraffe has very high blood pressure.
The pulse at your wrist comes from the left ventricle. The beat of the right ventricle goes only to your lungs.
explanations.art: A figure-of-eight diagram with the heart at the centre, a small pale loop to the lungs marked 'gentle push' and a large bold loop to the body marked 'strong push'.

explanations.definition: An artery carries blood away from the heart. A vein carries blood back to the heart. Capillaries are the thinnest vessels, and join the two.
explanations.description: Arteries have thick, stretchy, muscular walls, because the heart pushes the blood in them hard. Each beat makes an artery swell a little. That swelling is the pulse you feel at your wrist. Veins have thinner walls and small one-way valves, which stop the blood flowing backwards. The aorta is the biggest artery. It leaves the left ventricle and sends blood to the whole body. The carotid arteries run up each side of the neck to the head. The two venae cavae are the biggest veins. They bring blood from the body back to the right atrium. The pulmonary artery carries blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. The pulmonary veins bring blood from the lungs to the left atrium. Notice that the pulmonary artery carries blood that is low in oxygen. So an artery is not 'blood with oxygen', and a vein is not 'blood without oxygen'. The real difference is the direction: away from the heart, or back to it.
examples: The pulse at your wrist is an artery swelling with each beat.
The bluish lines on the back of a grandparent's hand are veins.
The aorta leaves the left ventricle, and the venae cavae enter the right atrium.
explanations.art: The heart in the middle with a thick red tube leaving the top, labelled aorta, two blue tubes entering the right side, labelled venae cavae, and small arrows to show direction.

explanations.concept: Capillaries leak, and lymph brings the liquid back
explanations.definition: A closed circulatory system is not perfectly closed. Watery liquid leaks out of the capillaries all the time, and thin tubes called lymph vessels return it to the blood.
explanations.description: A capillary wall is one cell thick, with tiny gaps. The pressure of the blood pushes some of the watery part out through the gaps. This liquid bathes the cells. It is how food and oxygen cover the last short distance from the blood to a cell. Most of the liquid goes back into the capillaries further along. In an adult, about 3 litres a day does not. Lymph vessels collect it and pour it back into large veins near the heart. No heart pumps the lymph. It is squeezed along when the muscles round the vessels move, and valves stop it from flowing backwards.
examples: Feet and ankles can swell after a long train journey, because sitting still does not squeeze the lymph along.
The clear liquid that oozes from a graze before it scabs is mostly this leaked liquid.
The 'glands' in your neck that swell with a sore throat are lymph nodes, where the lymph is checked for microbes.
explanations.art: A capillary passing between body cells with small drops leaking out, and a thin green tube with a valve in it collecting the drops.

explanations.concept: Heart attack: when an artery to the heart is blocked
explanations.definition: A heart attack happens when blood cannot get through an artery that feeds the heart muscle, so a part of the muscle runs short of oxygen.
explanations.description: The heart is a muscle, and it needs oxygen too. Its own arteries, called coronary arteries, run over its surface. Over many years, fat from food can build up inside artery walls and make them narrow. If a blood clot then blocks the narrow place, the heart muscle beyond it gets no oxygen and starts to die. This is a heart attack. Some people call it a heart stroke, but a stroke is a blocked or burst vessel in the brain. A heart attack is more common in older people. It is more likely if a person smokes, has high blood pressure, or often eats a lot of greasy, deep-fried food. The warning signs are pain or heaviness in the chest that may spread to the left arm or the jaw, sweating, and feeling sick or breathless. A person with these signs needs a doctor at once. Call an ambulance (112 in India) or take them to the nearest hospital. Eating less fried food, keeping ghee and oil to small amounts, walking every day and not smoking all lower the chance.
examples: A grandfather stops on the stairs with a heavy chest and sweating, and his family takes him to hospital straight away.
A narrow, fat-lined artery drawn beside a clear one.
explanations.art: Two arteries cut open, one clear and one narrowed by a yellow fatty lining with a red clot stuck in it.

explanations.concept: Looking after your lungs and heart
explanations.definition: Lungs and heart stay healthy when we keep smoke away, stay active, and sometimes breathe slowly and deeply.
explanations.description: Smoking bidi or cigarettes harms the alveoli. The smoke damages their thin walls and coats the tubes with sticky tar. Over the years, less oxygen can cross into the blood, and the person gets breathing diseases, such as a cough that never goes away. Other people's smoke harms children's lungs too. Exercise such as walking, cycling or playing kabaddi makes the heart muscle stronger, so it pushes more blood with each beat. Yoga has been practised in India for thousands of years. Doctors often advise yoga, and slow deep breathing called pranayama, as part of a healthy heart habit, because they calm the body and slow the heartbeat. A deep breath also changes more of the air in your lungs than a quiet breath does. But some air always stays, as you saw with residual air. These habits help, but they do not take the place of a doctor's advice.
examples: A grandfather who gave up bidi finds that he coughs less after a few months.
A morning walk, a game of kabaddi or a few minutes of slow breathing before bed.
A child who has an asthma inhaler still does yoga, but follows the doctor's advice first.
explanations.art: A grandmother doing slow breathing on a mat on a terrace at sunrise while a child cycles in the lane below.

explanations.definition: A gill is a set of very thin plates full of blood. Water flows between the plates in one direction, and oxygen dissolved in the water diffuses into the blood.
explanations.description: Water is hard to breathe for three reasons. First, it holds little oxygen. A litre of fresh water holds about 8 cubic centimetres of oxygen, and a litre of air holds about 210. Second, water is about 800 times as dense as air, so moving it takes much more work. Third, oxygen spreads through water thousands of times more slowly than through air. Gills deal with all three. The water never turns round. It comes in at the mouth and leaves behind the operculum, so the water never has to be stopped and sent back. The plates are extremely thin and very many. And the blood in them flows against the water, which you will meet on the next card. Gills fail in air because nothing holds the plates apart. In water each plate floats free. In air the wet plates cling together, and most of their surface is lost.
examples: A fish in a tank opens the mouth and the gill covers in turn. That is a pump with two chambers, pushing water one way.
Some sharks and tunas swim with the mouth open, and the swimming drives the water over the gills.
A wet paintbrush out of water clumps into a point, the way gill filaments do.
explanations.art: A fish's head cut away to show water entering the mouth, passing between rows of red gill plates and leaving behind the gill cover, with blue arrows for the water.

explanations.definition: In counter-flow exchange, blood and water flow in opposite directions on the two sides of a thin wall. All along the wall, the water has a little more oxygen than the blood next to it, so oxygen keeps crossing.
explanations.description: Oxygen diffuses only from where there is more to where there is less. Suppose blood and water flowed the same way. At the start the water would have much more oxygen, and oxygen would cross fast. Soon the two would hold equal amounts, and the crossing would stop. The blood could collect half the oxygen at most. Now turn the blood round. Blood that is nearly full meets the freshest water, which still has more oxygen than the blood has. Blood that is nearly empty meets water that is nearly used up, which still has a little more than the blood has. So oxygen crosses along the whole length. The gills of many fish take up about 80 parts in 100 of the oxygen in the water that passes over them.
examples: In the Bean Gill activity, the blood cup leaves with about 12 of 16 beans when it moves against the water, and never more than 8 when it moves with the water.
The legs of a wading bird, such as a flamingo at Pulicat Lake, use the same plan for heat. Warm blood going down passes cold blood coming up and warms it.
Engineers copy the plan in heat exchangers, which pass heat from one liquid to another in factories and power stations.
explanations.art: Two diagrams: on top, two arrows pointing the same way with dots that even out half-way along; below, two arrows pointing opposite ways with dots crossing along the whole length.

explanations.concept: Three heart plans: fish, frog and human
explanations.definition: A fish's heart has two chambers and pumps blood round one loop. A frog's heart has three chambers. A human heart has four chambers and pumps blood round two loops.
explanations.description: In a fish, one atrium receives the blood and one ventricle pumps it to the gills. From the gills it flows straight on to the body. The narrow gill capillaries take away much of the push, so the blood reaches the body at low pressure. That suits a fish, whose body is held up by the water. A frog has two atria and one ventricle. Blood from the lungs and skin and blood from the body partly mix in the ventricle. That suits a frog, who takes in much of their oxygen through the skin. In humans, the ventricle is divided in two. Blood from the lungs and blood from the body never mix, and each loop has a pump of its own. Birds and crocodiles also have four chambers. Birds and mammals came to this plan separately, from ancestors whose ventricle was not fully divided.
examples: Fish: 2 chambers, single circulation. Frog: 3 chambers. Crow, crocodile and human: 4 chambers, double circulation.
Most lizards, snakes and turtles have three chambers, with a ventricle that is partly divided.
In the Squirt Test, the water that has passed through cotton wool has lost its push, as blood has after the gills.
explanations.art: Three simple hearts in a row with their loops: a fish heart with two chambers and one loop, a frog heart with three chambers, and a human heart with four chambers and two loops.

explanations.concept: A frog breathes in three ways
explanations.definition: A tadpole breathes with gills. An adult frog breathes with lungs and also through thin, wet skin and the lining of the mouth.
explanations.description: A frog has no diaphragm. To fill the lungs, a frog lowers the floor of the mouth to draw air in through the nostrils. Then the frog shuts the nostrils and raises the floor of the mouth, and this pushes the air down into the lungs. You can see the throat pumping. The skin does a large share of the work. It is thin, it is full of capillaries, and it is kept wet with mucus, because oxygen must dissolve in water before it can cross. Under water in a cold pond, a resting frog can get all the oxygen they need through the skin. This is also why a frog dries out and dies quickly in hot sun, and why chemicals in water harm frogs so easily.
examples: Watch the throat of an Indian bullfrog after the first monsoon rain. It moves up and down many times a minute.
An earthworm has no lungs or gills and breathes only through damp skin.
Tadpoles in a rain puddle have gills. As legs grow, lungs grow too, and the gills are lost.
explanations.art: A frog sitting half in water with the throat puffed, small arrows of oxygen entering through the skin, and a tadpole with feathery gills swimming below.

explanations.concept: Bird lungs: air that flows one way
explanations.definition: A bird's lungs are stiff and do not swell and shrink. Thin bags called air sacs work as bellows and push air through the lungs in one direction.
explanations.description: Most birds have nine air sacs spread through the body. When a bird breathes in, fresh air goes mainly to the sacs at the back. When the bird breathes out, that fresh air is pushed forward through the lungs. So air moves through the lung tubes in the same direction during the breath in and the breath out. Fresh air does not mix with a large store of old air, as it does in our lungs. The blood flows across the path of the air, which also helps it collect oxygen. This is one reason birds can fly where the air is thin. Bar-headed geese fly over the Himalayas twice a year, between Central Asia and wetlands in India. Scientists who put trackers on them recorded one goose at 7,290 metres.
examples: A crow's tail bobs gently as the air sacs fill and empty.
Bar-headed geese spend the winter at lakes and fields from Assam to Tamil Nadu.
A bird has no diaphragm. Muscles of the ribs and belly move the breastbone to work the air sacs.
explanations.art: A goose in flight shown in outline, with small stiff lungs in the middle, large pale air sacs in front and behind, and arrows showing air passing one way through the lungs.

explanations.definition: In a closed circulatory system, blood stays inside vessels. In an open one, the heart pumps the liquid into the body spaces, where it washes over the organs directly.
explanations.description: A grasshopper's heart is a tube along the back. It pumps haemolymph forward and out into the space round the organs. The liquid drifts back and enters the heart again through small holes with valves. There are no capillaries. The pressure is low, and the liquid moves slowly. A closed system costs more to build and to run, because the heart must force blood through very narrow tubes. In return it can send blood fast, at high pressure, and it can send more to one organ and less to another. Insects, spiders, crabs, prawns and snails have open systems. Earthworms, octopuses, squids and all animals with backbones have closed ones. An earthworm has five pairs of muscular vessels that work as hearts.
examples: A cockroach can use the low pressure of an open system because their oxygen travels in air tubes, not in the haemolymph.
A spider straightens some leg joints by raising the pressure of the haemolymph.
An octopus, with a closed system and three hearts, can hunt fast. A garden snail, with an open system, lives slowly.
explanations.art: Two diagrams side by side: a ring of closed tubes with a heart, and a tube heart open at the front pouring liquid into a wide space filled with organs.

explanations.concept: Insects: air tubes, and blood that carries almost no oxygen
explanations.definition: An insect takes air in through spiracles and carries it through branching tracheae to every part of the body. The haemolymph of most insects plays almost no part in carrying oxygen.
explanations.description: The tracheae branch into finer and finer tubes. The tips are wet, and they end right beside the cells. Oxygen dissolves in that liquid and diffuses the last short distance into the cell. So in an insect, air is piped right to the cells. Oxygen spreads through air thousands of times faster than through water, which is why this works in a small body. Large or busy insects also pump. They squeeze the abdomen to push air along the big tubes, and they open some spiracles while closing others. The haemolymph carries food, waste, hormones and cells that fight microbes. This shows that carrying oxygen is one job blood can have, and not what makes a liquid blood.
examples: Watch a resting grasshopper or wasp. The abdomen pulses in and out as the insect pumps air.
Many mosquito larvae hang head-down from the surface of still water and breathe air through a tube at the tail end.
A few insects, such as the red larvae of some midges, do have haemoglobin. It helps them live in mud with very little oxygen.
explanations.art: A grasshopper drawn in outline with a row of dots along the side, silver tubes branching inward from each dot, and a magnified circle showing a tube tip touching a muscle cell.

explanations.concept: Blood of other colours, and blood with no colour
explanations.definition: Animals carry oxygen with different molecules. Haemoglobin, with iron, is red. Haemocyanin, with copper, is blue when it carries oxygen. A few animals carry oxygen with no such molecule.
explanations.description: In your blood, haemoglobin is packed inside red blood cells. In an earthworm, haemoglobin floats free in the liquid of the blood. In octopuses, crabs and snails, haemocyanin floats free, and the blood looks pale blue. An octopus has three hearts. Two push blood through the two gills, and the third pushes it round the body. The strangest blood belongs to the icefishes of the sea round Antarctica. As adults they have no haemoglobin, and their blood is clear. Oxygen is simply dissolved in the watery part. This carries less than a fifth as much oxygen as the blood of related fishes. Icefishes manage with very cold water, which holds more oxygen, and with a large heart that pumps a large amount of blood.
examples: Human: red blood, haemoglobin inside cells. Earthworm: red blood, haemoglobin loose in the liquid.
Octopus, crab and snail: blue blood, with haemocyanin.
Antarctic icefish: clear blood, with no haemoglobin at all.
explanations.art: Four drops in a row labelled human, earthworm, octopus and icefish, coloured red, red, pale blue and clear.

explanations.concept: Is one way of breathing better than another?
explanations.definition: There is no agreed ranking of breathing organs or blood systems. Scientists compare them one job at a time.
explanations.description: Books often arrange animals in a line, from 'simple' hearts and gills to 'advanced' four-chambered hearts and lungs. Most biologists today do not accept that line. Here are the main views.
examples: A fish's gills take a larger share of the oxygen from water than your lungs take from air.
A bird's lungs work at heights where a human climber needs bottled oxygen.
There are more kinds of insect, with open blood and air tubes, than of all other animals together.

perspectives.explanation: Animals can be ranked. Two chambers are simple, three are in between, and four are the most advanced. On this view our own body is the finished design.

Each plan fits a way of life. A fish heart suits a body held up by water. Tidal lungs waste some of each breath but lose little water. No plan is the top of a ladder, and every animal alive today has ancestors as old as ours.

You can still compare how well each design does one job. For taking oxygen out of what flows past, bird lungs and fish gills beat ours. For keeping blood pressure high, a closed system beats an open one. 'Better' always needs the question 'better at what?'

explanations.art: A fish, a frog, a grasshopper, a goose and a child standing side by side on one level line, with no steps or ladder between them.

agreed.text: Oxygen passes from the air in the lungs into the blood by diffusion alone. No cell pumps it across.
agreed.evidence: In 1910 August and Marie Krogh measured the oxygen in lung air and in the blood leaving the lungs. The lung air always had the higher oxygen pressure. In 1915 Marie Krogh measured how fast a gas crosses a human lung, and diffusion was fast enough to explain all of it.

agreed.text: The lungs never empty. A quiet breath changes only a small part of the air in them.
agreed.evidence: Doctors measure the air left in the lungs by having a person breathe a known amount of a harmless gas, such as helium, and seeing how much it is thinned. Breathed-out air still holds about 16 parts of oxygen in 100, against 21 in room air.

agreed.text: In fish gills, blood flows against the water, and the gills take up most of the oxygen in the water passing over them.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have measured the oxygen in water just before and just after it crosses the gills. Many fish take up about 80 parts in 100. Under a microscope, the blood in the gill plates can be seen to run in the opposite direction to the water.

agreed.text: In animals with backbones, blood stays inside vessels and goes round and round. Arteries and veins are joined by capillaries.
agreed.evidence: William Harvey showed in 1628 that the blood must go round. In 1661 Marcello Malpighi looked at a frog's lung through a microscope and saw the capillaries that join the arteries to the veins.

agreed.text: Air flows one way through a bird's lungs, both when the bird breathes in and when the bird breathes out.
agreed.evidence: In 1971 scientists placed tiny flow sensors in the airways of ducks and recorded which way the air moved during each part of a breath.

agreed.text: Insects carry oxygen as a gas in air tubes, and many of them pump air through the tubes.
agreed.evidence: The air tubes can be seen under a microscope, ending beside the cells. In 2003 scientists used strong X-rays to film living beetles, ants and crickets, and saw the main tubes being squeezed and released in a rhythm.

challenging.claim: Each breath fills your lungs with fresh air and then empties them.
challenging.for: It feels that way. Air goes in, the chest rises, air goes out, the chest falls.
challenging.against: About a litre of air cannot be breathed out at all, and more stays after a quiet breath. Each new breath is mixed into it. That is why breathed-out air still has about 16 parts of oxygen in 100.
challenging.context: This card is about what happens to the air inside your lungs from one breath to the next.

challenging.claim: A fish dies in air because air does not have the kind of oxygen a fish can use.
challenging.for: Fish live in water and take oxygen from water, so it seems that air must be useless to them.
challenging.against: The oxygen in air and the oxygen dissolved in water are the same substance, and air holds far more of it. Out of water, the wet plates of the gills cling together and dry, so there is hardly any surface left for oxygen to cross. Fish such as the murrel and the climbing perch have an extra organ that stays open in air, and they can breathe air for hours.
challenging.context: This card is about why a fish suffocates out of water.

challenging.claim: A four-chambered heart is the most advanced heart, and the hearts of fish and frogs are primitive.
challenging.for: Four chambers keep blood from the lungs and blood from the body fully apart, which allows a high blood pressure and a busy, warm body.
challenging.against: A fish's heart suits a fish. A frog's mixed blood suits an animal who takes in oxygen through the skin and can stay under water for a long time without using the lungs. Fish and frogs alive today have as long a history behind them as we have.
challenging.context: This card is about whether hearts can be ranked from simple to advanced.

challenging.claim: The cells of the lung actively push oxygen into the blood, the way a gland pushes out sweat.
challenging.who: Christian Bohr and John Scott Haldane, around 1900
challenging.for: Their measurements seemed to show more oxygen pressure in the blood than in the lung air. Haldane also thought that secretion would explain how people get used to high mountains.
challenging.against: August and Marie Krogh made more careful measurements from 1910 and found the oxygen pressure always higher in the lung air. Later work on mountains agreed with them. Diffusion alone is enough.
challenging.context: This card is about how oxygen gets from the air in the lungs into the blood.

challenging.claim: Blood is the liquid that carries oxygen, so every animal's blood must carry oxygen.
challenging.for: In humans and all other animals with backbones, carrying oxygen is one of the main jobs of blood.
challenging.against: In most insects the haemolymph carries almost no oxygen, because air tubes take it straight to the cells. The haemolymph still carries food, waste and hormones. So blood is better described as the liquid a body moves round to carry things.
challenging.context: This card is about what blood is for in different animals.

big_questions.q: Some of the air in your lungs has been there for many breaths. Where does one breath end and the next begin?
big_questions.hint: Think about the tumbler in the Half-Breath Test after three pours. Which pour did its water come from?

big_questions.q: In a grasshopper, blood and the liquid round the cells are one liquid. In you they are two. Is your blood really shut in?
big_questions.hint: Remember the liquid that leaks from your capillaries and comes back as lymph.

big_questions.q: A gill only works with water between its plates. Is the water part of the gill?
big_questions.hint: Think about the paintbrush in water and out of it.

big_questions.q: A fish, a frog, a grasshopper and a goose solve the same problem in four ways. Is it right to call any of them the best?
big_questions.hint: Ask 'best at what?' and 'best for whom?' before you answer.

big_questions.q: Marie and August Krogh had to tell August's own teacher that he was wrong. When is it right to disagree with a teacher?
big_questions.hint: Think about what they did before they said it. They measured again and again.

big_questions.q: The oxygen you are breathing was made by plants, algae and microbes. Whose breath is it?
big_questions.hint: Follow one oxygen particle backwards from your lung to a leaf or a drop of sea water.

story.title: The Well That Had to Breathe
story.note: Malar, Pechi paatti, Murugan and this well are made up. These facts are real. Carbon dioxide and other gases can collect at the bottom of a well, and people die in wells every year because of them. Oxfam's guide to cleaning hand-dug wells tells workers to lower a lighted candle before anyone goes in, and not to enter if the flame goes out. The same guide says that lowering and raising a large bundle of twigs or branches can help to clear the air. A flame does not warn of every dangerous gas. No child should ever go into a well, a tank or a pit, and no adult should without training and a rope.
text: The well behind Pechi paatti's house was forty feet deep, and in the month of Vaikasi it was nearly dry.

That was the time to clean it. Every summer someone went down with a basket and a short spade and sent up the mud and the rotted leaves, so that the spring at the bottom could run clear again. For forty summers that someone had been Paatti. This year her knees had said no. Malar's cousin Murugan, who was sixteen and could climb a coconut palm in the time it took to say so, was going instead.
'Not yet,' said Paatti.

She lit the small brass lamp, set it in a wire basket and let it down on a rope. Malar lay on her stomach at the edge and watched. The flame went down steady and yellow, past the first ring of stones, past the fig root that grew out of the wall, past the green line where the water had stood in December. Then, a little above the mud, it shrank to a blue bead and went out.
'Bad air,' said Paatti, and pulled the lamp up. 'Nobody goes down.'
'The rope shook it,' said Murugan.
'Then you hold the rope.'
He held it as still as a heron. The flame went out at the same place.

That had been Monday. Paatti took the palm-leaf lid off the well and said the bad air would go by itself, now that the well was open to the sky. On Tuesday the lamp went out a little above the mud. On Wednesday it went out a little above the mud.
'Three days with the lid off,' Murugan said. 'A room airs out in an hour.'
'A room has a door and a window,' said Malar. She had not known she was going to say it.

She was thinking about the afternoon wind. It had been blowing since two o'clock. It shook the neem tree and lifted the washing and rolled a dry leaf across the yard to the well. She watched the leaf tip over the edge. It did not blow about down there. It fell slowly and straight, turning, all the way to the mud, as if there were no wind anywhere in the world.
The wind crossed the mouth of the well and went on. It could not push new air in, because the air already inside had no other way out.

Then she thought of the kudam. Every morning she rinsed the brass water pot, the one with the narrow neck. If she only let a little clean water run in at the top, the cloudy water at the bottom stayed where it was. She had to pour some in, and swirl it, and pour it out, and do it again, and again. Each time the water came out only a little cleaner than before. Seven or eight times, on a bad day.
'Paatti,' she said, 'the well has only one mouth. We have to rinse it.'
Paatti looked at her for a while. Then she sent Murugan up the neem tree with the sickle.

They tied the cut branches into a bundle nearly as wide as the well, leaves and all, and hung it on the rope over the pulley. Malar and Murugan let it down to the bottom and hauled it up to the top, and let it down, and hauled it up. Going down, the bundle pushed the air below it up past its edges. Coming up, it drew air from the yard down behind it. Dust came out of the well as they worked, and the smell of wet stone.
After thirty pulls their arms shook. Paatti lowered the lamp. It burned a hand's width lower than before, and went out.
'It did nothing,' said Murugan.
'It did a hand's width,' said Malar. 'The first rinse never cleans the pot.'

Thirty more. The lamp went out just above the mud, but slowly this time, the flame leaning and thinning before it died. Thirty more, with Paatti counting aloud and the neighbour's daughter taking a turn on the rope. Malar's palms were red. A crow sat on the pulley post and watched the bundle go by, down and up, down and up.
At the fourth try the lamp reached the bottom and stood on the mud, small and yellow. Nobody spoke. Paatti counted to one hundred under her breath. The flame was still there.

'Now,' said Paatti. 'With the rope round your waist. The lamp stays down there beside you, and you look at it more than you look at the mud. If it goes blue, you come up, and you do not fill the basket first.' She turned to Malar. 'And the air does not stop moving.'

So Murugan went down, and the mud came up basket by basket, black and smelling of old rain. All that afternoon a smaller bundle of neem went on travelling down one side of the well and up again. Down. Up. Down. Up.

Malar pulled until the light turned orange. Somewhere after the two hundredth pull she noticed that she was breathing in as the bundle rose and out as it fell. She could not have said which of them had started copying the other.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the story never mentions lungs, but the well is built like one. It has a single opening, so wind across the top does not change the air at the bottom. Air has to be moved in and out through the same mouth, many times, and each time only part of the old air is changed. That is why the lamp burned only a hand's width lower after the first thirty pulls. Malar gets there by remembering how a narrow-necked pot is rinsed. Do not explain the link at once. Ask the questions below and let your child find it.
ask: Why did three days of wind not change the air at the bottom of the well?
Why did the lamp burn only a little lower after the first thirty pulls?
Which part of your body has one opening for air going in and coming out?
How is rinsing a narrow-necked pot like the Half-Breath Test?
What would be different if the well had a second opening near the bottom?

games.title: Build a Body: match the animal, the breathing and the blood
games.context: This is a card game about eight animals. Each animal has a way of breathing and a kind of blood system. You collect the three cards that belong to one body, and you say why they fit together.

printables.title: 24 body cards: 8 animals, 8 ways of breathing and 8 blood systems
items: BREATHING. Lungs with millions of air sacs. A diaphragm pulls air in. Air goes in and out by one path.
BREATHING. Gills under a hard cover. Water flows one way, against the blood.
BREATHING. Lungs filled by pumping the throat. Thin, wet skin does a large share.
BREATHING. Stiff lungs and nine air sacs. Air flows one way through the lungs.
BREATHING. Spiracles along the sides, and air tubes that reach every cell.
BREATHING. No lungs and no gills. Only thin, damp skin.
BREATHING. Two gills inside a bag of muscle that pumps water in and out.
BREATHING. Gills kept wet inside a shell. A small paddle drives water over them.
BLOOD. Closed. A heart with four chambers. Two loops.
BLOOD. Closed. A heart with four chambers. Two loops. (second copy)
BLOOD. Closed. A heart with two chambers. One loop.
BLOOD. Closed. A heart with three chambers. Blood from lungs and body partly mixes.
BLOOD. Open. A tube heart along the back. The liquid carries almost no oxygen.
BLOOD. Closed. Five pairs of hearts. Red blood with no red blood cells.
BLOOD. Closed. Three hearts. Blue blood.
BLOOD. Open. Blue liquid that does carry oxygen.

printables.title: Answer sheet: the 8 bodies
items: Human child: lungs with air sacs and a diaphragm. Closed, four chambers, two loops.
Rohu: gills under a hard cover. Closed, two chambers, one loop.
Indian bullfrog: lungs filled by the throat, and wet skin. Closed, three chambers.
Bar-headed goose: stiff lungs and nine air sacs. Closed, four chambers, two loops.
Grasshopper: spiracles and air tubes. Open, tube heart, liquid with almost no oxygen.
Earthworm: damp skin only. Closed, five pairs of hearts, red blood with no red blood cells.
Octopus: two gills in a bag of muscle. Closed, three hearts, blue blood.
Mud crab: gills inside a shell with a paddle. Open, blue liquid that carries oxygen.

rules: For 2 to 4 players. Shuffle the 24 cards. Deal 4 to each player. Put the rest face down in a pile.
On your turn, take the top card of the pile, or the top card of the throw-away heap.
If you now hold one ANIMAL card and the BREATHING and BLOOD cards that match, lay the three down. Say one reason why they fit.
The other players check the answer sheet. If the body is wrong, take the cards back into your hand.
End your turn by putting one card face up on the throw-away heap.
The first player to lay down two bodies wins. If the pile runs out, shuffle the throw-away heap and use it again.
Playing alone: lay all 24 cards face up and build the 8 bodies. Time yourself, then check the answer sheet.

flow.say: Each animal has one breathing card and one blood card. Two animals share the same kind of blood card. Can you guess which two?

ask.q: Why can a grasshopper manage with slow, open blood?
good: The air tubes take oxygen straight to the cells.
The blood does not have to carry oxygen, so it need not be fast.

ask.q: The human and the goose have the same blood card. What is different about their breathing?
good: Our air goes in and out the same way.
The goose's air flows one way through the lungs.

flow.parent: Accept any true reason. If a player lays a wrong body, ask which card does not fit and why. The frog and the earthworm are often mixed up, because both use the skin.

flow.do: 1. Lay all 8 bodies out in a row, using the answer sheet. 2. Sort them into open blood and closed blood. 3. Then sort them by what they breathe: air or water.
flow.say: Sort the bodies two ways. Do all the water breathers have the same kind of blood? Do all the air breathers?
flow.kid: Lay out all 8 bodies. Sort them by blood. Then sort them by air or water.
flow.think: The crab and the octopus both breathe water with gills. Why might the octopus need closed blood and three hearts?
flow.context: This is the last step of Build a Body. You sort the eight bodies in two different ways.

games.title: Three Clues: who breathes like this?
games.context: This is a guessing game about how different animals get oxygen. Each card has three clues, from hard to easy. The sooner you guess the animal, the more points you get.

printables.title: 12 clue cards: three clues on the front, the animal on the back

items.f: Clue 1: My lungs are stiff, and air flows one way through them. Clue 2: I cross the Himalayas twice a year. Clue 3: I am a goose with two dark bars on my head.
items.b: Bar-headed goose. Scientists tracked one flying at 7,290 metres.

items.f: Clue 1: My blood is clear, with no haemoglobin. Clue 2: The water I live in is close to freezing. Clue 3: I am a fish of the sea round Antarctica.
items.b: Icefish. Oxygen is carried dissolved in the watery part of the blood.

items.f: Clue 1: I breathe air through a tube at my tail end. Clue 2: I hang from the surface of still water. Clue 3: When I grow up I will fly, and the females of my kind bite.
items.b: Mosquito larva. A film of oil or a tight lid on the water stops the larva from reaching air.

items.f: Clue 1: I have three hearts. Clue 2: My blood is blue, with copper in it. Clue 3: I have eight arms.
items.b: Octopus. Two hearts serve the two gills, and one serves the body.

items.f: Clue 1: I have no lungs and no gills. Clue 2: I have five pairs of hearts. Clue 3: I come up onto wet ground after heavy rain.
items.b: Earthworm. Oxygen crosses the damp skin into red blood.

items.f: Clue 1: I began life with gills and lost them. Clue 2: I fill my lungs by pumping my throat. Clue 3: I call loudly after the first monsoon rain.
items.b: Frog. The skin does a large share of the breathing.

items.f: Clue 1: I am a fish, but I come to the surface to gulp air. Clue 2: I can stay alive for hours in a damp basket. Clue 3: In Tamil Nadu I am sold as viral, and in the north as a kind of murrel.
items.b: Murrel, a snakehead fish. A folded organ above the gills takes oxygen from gulped air.

items.f: Clue 1: I must keep swimming so that water flows over my gills. Clue 2: I have no bony gill cover, only slits. Clue 3: My skeleton is cartilage and I have many rows of teeth.
items.b: Shark. Many sharks drive water over the gills by swimming with the mouth open.

items.f: Clue 1: Air reaches my cells through tubes, and my blood carries almost no oxygen. Clue 2: My heart is a tube along my back. Clue 3: I jump with long back legs and eat leaves.
items.b: Grasshopper. The abdomen pumps to move air along the tubes.

items.f: Clue 1: I breathe air with lungs, but I live in the sea. Clue 2: My nostril is on the top of my head. Clue 3: I am a mammal who leaps and clicks.
items.b: Dolphin. A dolphin changes most of the air in the lungs with each fast breath.

items.f: Clue 1: My heart pushes blood about two metres up to my brain. Clue 2: My blood pressure is among the highest of all animals. Clue 3: I have a very long neck.
items.b: Giraffe. A closed system with a strong left ventricle makes this possible.

items.f: Clue 1: My lungs were full of liquid until today. Clue 2: Until today, my oxygen came through a cord. Clue 3: I have just cried for the first time.
items.b: A newborn human baby. With the first breaths, air replaces the liquid, and the lungs never empty again.

rules: Shuffle the 12 cards and put them in a pile, clue side up.
One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads clue 1 aloud.
The guesser may name one animal. If it is right, the guesser scores 3 points.
If not, the reader reads clue 2. A right guess now scores 2 points. After clue 3, it scores 1 point.
After each card, the reader reads the back aloud. Then swap jobs.
Play all 12 cards. The player with the most points wins.
Playing alone: cover the card with a sheet of paper. Slide it down one clue at a time, and keep your own score.

flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Stack them clue side up. Choose who reads first.

ask.q: Which clue told you the most, and why?
good: The one about the heart, because few animals have three.
The one about air tubes, because only insects and their relatives have them.

flow.kid: Add up your points. Pick the card that surprised you. Say why that body works.
