experiments.title: The Half-Breath Test: how many breaths does it take to change the air in a lung?
experiments.context: In this experiment a tumbler of dark water stands for a lung full of used air. Clean water stands for fresh air. Like a lung, the tumbler has one opening, so you can only pour some out and put some in. You count how many 'breaths' it takes to make the water clear.
experiments.question: If each breath changes half of what is in the tumbler, how many breaths does it take before the dark water looks as clear as clean water? What if each breath changes only a quarter?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Each breath, you will pour out half of the dark water, fill the tumbler up with clean water and stir. How many breaths will it take until you cannot tell it from clean water? Why do you think so? Write your guess and your reason.
experiments.fair_test: The dark water is made once, in one jug, and used for every run. The tumbler is filled to the same top line each time and stirred five times after each filling. The same person judges the colour, against the same white paper, beside the same tumbler of clean water. Only the size of the breath changes: half in the first run, a quarter in the second.

materials.item: 2 clear tumblers or glasses with straight sides, of the same size. Two clear plastic bottles with the tops cut off by a grown-up also work
strong black tea or coffee decoction, about 2 tumblers, cooled. A few drops of food colouring or ink in water also work
a jug of clean water and a bucket or sink to pour into
a ruler and a marker pen, or 3 rubber bands, to mark lines on the tumbler
a spoon for stirring
a sheet of white paper
a notebook and a pencil

experiments.safety: A grown-up makes the tea and lets it cool fully before the test starts.

schedule.what: Mark the tumbler. Guess, then count the breaths needed to clear the dark water with half-breaths and with quarter-breaths. Predict the count for a smaller breath, and say what you found.

experiments.record: Fill in the results table. Under it, write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: breaths needed to clear the tumbler
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: A straight-sided clear glass with three marker lines on it at 8, 6 and 4 centimetres from the bottom, beside a ruler.
setup.caption: 1. Mark three lines on one tumbler: 8, 6 and 4 centimetres up from the bottom.

setup.art: Two glasses on a sheet of white paper, one full of dark brown tea to the top line and one full of clean water.
setup.caption: 2. Fill the marked tumbler with dark water to the top line. Fill the other with clean water.

setup.art: A child pouring dark water from the marked glass into a bucket until the level reaches the middle line.
setup.caption: 3. One breath: pour out down to the 4 centimetre line.

setup.art: The same child topping the glass up with clean water from a jug and stirring with a spoon, the liquid now paler.
setup.caption: 4. Fill up with clean water to the top line. Stir. Compare with the clean tumbler, and count.

flow.do: 1. Stand the ruler beside one tumbler. 2. Mark lines at 8, 6 and 4 centimetres from the bottom. 3. Fill it with dark water to the 8 centimetre line. 4. Fill the other tumbler with clean water.
flow.say: This dark tumbler is a lung full of used air. The clean water in the jug is fresh air. The tumbler has only one opening, like a lung.
flow.kid: Mark three lines on one tumbler. Fill it with dark water. Fill the other with clean water.
flow.parent: The tea should be as dark as strong black tea without milk. The 4 centimetre line is half of the 8 centimetre filling, and the 6 centimetre line is three quarters. Stand both tumblers on white paper near a window.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Half-Breath Test. You set up a tumbler of dark water to stand for a lung.

flow.do: 1. Explain one breath: pour out down to the 4 centimetre line, fill up with clean water, stir. 2. Ask how many breaths will make it look like clean water. 3. Ask for the reason. 4. Write both down.
flow.say: One breath changes half the water. How many breaths until you cannot tell it from the clean tumbler? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: One breath changes half the water. Guess how many breaths will clear it. Say why.

ask.q: Why do you think it will take that many?
good: Two, because half and half makes a whole.
More than two, because the new water gets mixed with the old.
It may never be fully clear.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. 'Two' is the most common answer from children and from adults. Write it in the table with the reason.
flow.context: This is the second step of the Half-Breath Test. You guess how many half-breaths will clear the dark water.

flow.do: 1. Pour out down to the 4 centimetre line. 2. Fill up to the 8 centimetre line with clean water and stir five times. 3. Compare the two tumblers from the side, against the white paper. 4. Repeat, counting, until they look the same.
flow.say: That was breath one. Is it clear? Look from the side. Keep going, and count each breath aloud.
flow.kid: Pour out to the middle line. Fill up and stir. Compare. Count each breath until it looks clear.
flow.parent: Most families count between 6 and 9 half-breaths. The exact number depends on how dark the tea was and how sharp the judge's eyes are. Weak tea clears sooner. What matters is that it takes many more than two.

check.q: In the Half-Breath Test, how much of the first dark water is left after two half-breaths?
check.why: The first breath leaves half. The second breath pours out half of that, which leaves a quarter. If you chose 'none', you added the two halves. But the second pour takes out mixed water, and half of it is the clean water you had just put in.

flow.context: In this step of the Half-Breath Test, you change half the water again and again and count until it looks clear.

flow.do: 1. Empty the tumbler and fill it with dark water to the 8 centimetre line again. 2. Ask for a new guess and a reason. 3. This time pour out only to the 6 centimetre line each breath. 4. Fill up, stir, compare and count as before.
flow.say: Now each breath changes only a quarter. That is a quieter breath. How many will it take this time? Why?
flow.kid: Fill it with dark water again. Now pour out only to the 6 line. Guess, then count.
flow.parent: Most families count between 13 and 18 quarter-breaths, about twice the first count. It is slow, and the slowness is the finding. Let your child feel how many pours it takes.
flow.context: In this step of the Half-Breath Test, each breath changes only a quarter of the water, and you count again.

flow.do: 1. Put the two counts side by side. 2. Ask what pattern your child sees. 3. Ask them to predict the count if each breath changed one eighth. 4. If there is time, test it by pouring out only to the 7 centimetre line.
flow.say: Half took this many, and a quarter took this many. What do you notice? What would one eighth take?
flow.kid: Look at your two counts. What pattern do you see? Predict the count for one eighth.
flow.parent: Halving the size of the breath roughly doubles the number of breaths. So an eighth should take about 30. Testing it takes about ten minutes of pouring, so it is optional.
flow.context: In this step of the Half-Breath Test, you look for a pattern in your two counts and use it to predict a third.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. 2. Ask how the tumbler is like a lung and how it is different. 3. After they have answered, read the note below aloud.
flow.say: Say what you guessed, what you saw, and why you think it happened. Then tell me one way this tumbler is like your lungs.
flow.kid: Say what you guessed. Say what you saw. Say why. How is the tumbler like a lung?

ask.q: Why did it take so many breaths?
good: Each pour took out clean water as well as dark water.
The new water mixed with the old before the next pour.
Only part was changed each time.

ask.q: What does this model leave out?
good: Blood takes oxygen out of the air all the time.
Real lungs are not stirred with a spoon.
Real air is a gas, and it mixes faster.

flow.parent: The note to read: your lungs have one opening too. After a quiet breath out, an adult's lungs still hold about 2 litres of air. The next breath brings only about 350 millilitres of new air to the alveoli. That is roughly one seventh. So the air deep in your lungs is always a mixture, with less oxygen than room air. A fish's gill is different. Water goes in at the mouth and out behind the gill cover, so old water never mixes with new.
flow.think: A sigh or a yawn is a very big breath. What might a big breath do for the air deep in your lungs?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Half-Breath Test. You say what you found and compare the tumbler with a real lung.

experiments.title: The Squirt Test: what happens to the push after blood squeezes through capillaries?
experiments.context: In this experiment a squeeze bottle stands for a ventricle of the heart, and a plug of cotton wool stands for a bed of capillaries. You measure how far the water squirts with the plug and without it. It shows what happens to the pressure of the blood in a fish, whose heart pumps blood through the gills and straight on to the body.
experiments.question: A squeeze bottle squirts water a long way. If the water must first pass through a plug of cotton wool, how far does it squirt? What gets the push back?
experiments.predict: Guess first. With no plug, mark where you think the water will land. Then guess where it will land when it must pass through cotton wool first: the same place, half as far, or much less than half? Why do you think so? Write your guesses and your reason.
experiments.fair_test: The same bottle, filled to the same level, is squeezed by the same person with both hands as hard as they can. The bottle is held level at the same height, at the same starting line, every time. Each set-up is tried three times, and the farthest landing place of each try is measured. Only the plug changes.

materials.item: a soft plastic squeeze bottle with a nozzle cap, such as an empty dish-wash or sauce bottle, washed well. A soft water bottle with a small hole made in the cap by a grown-up also works
cotton wool, a ball about the size of a lemon
a steel tumbler to catch water, and a jug of water
a measuring tape or a ruler, and chalk
a place that can get wet: a bathroom, a balcony or a terrace
a notebook and a pencil

experiments.safety: The floor will be wet and slippery, so walk and do not run. A grown-up makes the hole if a bottle cap needs one. Never squirt at a person's face.

schedule.what: Guess. Measure how far the bottle squirts with no plug and with a cotton-wool plug. Catch the water that came through the plug, squeeze it again, and say what you found.

experiments.record: Fill in the results table. Draw a bar chart of the three farthest distances. Under it, write what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: how far the water squirted
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: A child on a balcony holding a squeeze bottle level at waist height, standing on a chalk line, with a jet of water arcing forward onto the floor.
setup.caption: 1. Stand on a chalk line. Hold the bottle level and squeeze hard. Mark where the water lands.

setup.art: A close view of hands pushing a ball of cotton wool firmly into the neck of the bottle before the cap goes on.
setup.caption: 2. Pack cotton wool firmly into the neck. Put the cap back on.

setup.art: The same child squeezing the bottle with the plug in, and the water dribbling out to land close to her feet.
setup.caption: 3. Squeeze again from the same line. Measure how far it goes now.

setup.art: Water that came through the plug being caught in a steel tumbler, and a second view of it being poured back into the open bottle.
setup.caption: 4. Catch the water that came through. Put it in the bottle with no plug, and squeeze once more.

flow.do: 1. Draw a chalk line on the floor. 2. Fill the bottle three quarters full. 3. Ask for a guess of where the water will land with no plug, and with a plug. 4. Ask for the reason. Mark both guesses with chalk.
flow.say: This bottle is a heart's ventricle. The cotton wool will be the capillaries of a gill. Where will the water land each time? Why?
flow.kid: Draw a start line. Guess where the water will land. Guess again for the plug. Say why.

ask.q: Why do you think the plug will change the distance?
good: The water has to push through tiny gaps.
It will slow the water down.
Some of the push gets used up in the cotton.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guesses. Many children expect the plug to make only a small difference.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Squirt Test. You guess how far a squeeze bottle will squirt with and without a plug.

flow.do: 1. Stand with toes on the line. 2. Hold the bottle level at waist height. 3. Squeeze as hard as you can with both hands. 4. Mark the farthest wet spot, and measure from the line. Do it three times.
flow.say: Squeeze as hard as you can, the same way each time. I will mark the farthest spot.
flow.kid: Stand on the line. Hold the bottle level. Squeeze hard. Do it three times.
flow.parent: Refill the bottle to the same level before each try. A dish-wash bottle usually squirts between 1 and 3 metres. Measure to the far end of the wet streak.

check.q: In the Squirt Test, why do you squeeze three times for each set-up?
options: The bottle works better when warm
One squeeze can be a fluke
check.why: No two squeezes are exactly alike. Three tries show how much the result changes when nothing else is changed. If you chose 'works better when warm', check your own numbers to see whether the later tries really went farther.

flow.context: In this step of the Squirt Test, you measure how far the bottle squirts with nothing in the way.

flow.do: 1. Take off the cap. 2. Pack cotton wool firmly into the neck, about two finger-widths deep. 3. Put the cap on. 4. Squeeze from the same line, three times, and measure.
flow.say: Now the water must pass through thousands of tiny gaps before it gets out. Squeeze just as hard. What happens?
flow.kid: Pack cotton wool into the neck. Squeeze just as hard. Measure three times.
flow.parent: The jet usually falls to less than half its distance, and often to a dribble. If it hardly changes, pack in more cotton wool, more tightly. If no water comes at all, loosen it a little.
flow.context: In this step of the Squirt Test, the water must pass through a cotton-wool plug before it leaves the bottle.

flow.do: 1. Squeeze the plugged bottle into the tumbler until the tumbler is half full. 2. Take the plug out of the bottle. 3. Pour the caught water back in. 4. Squeeze from the line again and measure.
flow.say: This water has been through the plug and lost its push. How could we give it a strong push again? Try it.
flow.kid: Catch the water that came through. Put it in the open bottle. Squeeze again and measure.
flow.parent: The second squeeze sends the water as far as in the first test. This is the second pump. In your body, the left ventricle gives it.
flow.context: In this step of the Squirt Test, you give the water a second squeeze after it has passed through the plug.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why. 2. Ask which animal's blood is like step 3, and which is like step 4. 3. After they have answered, read the note below aloud.
flow.say: Say what you guessed, what you saw, and why you think it happened. Which part was like a fish, and which was like you?
flow.kid: Say what you guessed. Say what you saw. Say why. Which step was like a fish?

good: It was used up forcing water through the tiny gaps.
Rubbing against the cotton slowed the water.

ask.q: Why does your heart have two ventricles?
good: One pushes blood through the lungs.
The other gives it a new push to reach the body.

flow.parent: The note to read: a fish's heart has one ventricle. It pushes blood through the capillaries of the gills, and the blood goes on to the body with much of its push used up. Your blood comes back to the heart after the lungs and gets a second, stronger push. The model leaves out a lot. Real capillaries are open tubes, not tangled fibres, and a fish's blood still flows steadily. A fish in water does not need high pressure.
flow.think: The right ventricle pushes gently and the left one pushes hard. What might happen to the thin lung capillaries if the right one pushed hard too?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Squirt Test. You say what you found and compare the bottle with a fish's heart and your own.

activities.title: The Paintbrush Gill: what does air do to a gill?
activities.context: This is a short activity to do before any explaining. A soft paintbrush stands for the fine threads of a fish's gill. You look at it in water and out of water, and you ask why a fish suffocates in air.

materials.item: a soft paintbrush, the wider the better. A fringe cut into a strip of thin cotton cloth also works
a clear tumbler of water
a ruler
a notebook and a pencil

activities.record: Write the width of the brush tip in water and in air. Write one thing you notice and one thing you wonder. Draw what you think happens to a fish's gills in air.

setup.art: A soft paintbrush held upright in a clear tumbler of water, with its hairs spread wide apart and a ruler held against the glass.
setup.caption: 1. Hold the brush in water. Look at the hairs. Measure how wide the tip spreads.

setup.art: The same paintbrush lifted just above the water, its wet hairs stuck together in a narrow point with a drop hanging from it.
setup.caption: 2. Lift it out slowly. Look again, and measure the tip.

setup.art: A notebook page with two small drawings of the brush, one spread and one clumped, and the words 'I notice' and 'I wonder'.
setup.caption: 3. Write what you notice and what you wonder.

flow.do: 1. Say that a litre of air holds about 26 times as much oxygen as a litre of pond water. 2. Ask why a fish suffocates in air. 3. Ask for a reason. Write it down.
flow.say: Air holds far more oxygen than water does. So why does a fish suffocate in air? What do you think, and why?
flow.kid: Air holds more oxygen than water. So why does a fish suffocate in air? Guess, and say why.

ask.q: Why do you think a fish suffocates in air?
good: Fish need water oxygen, not air oxygen.
The gills dry up.
A fish has no lungs to pull air in.

flow.parent: Do not correct any guess. 'Fish need a different kind of oxygen' is very common, and the unit comes back to it.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Paintbrush Gill. You guess why a fish suffocates in air.

flow.do: 1. Hold the brush upright in the tumbler, hairs under water. 2. Look from the side and measure how wide the tip spreads. 3. Lift it out slowly. 4. Measure the tip again. Dip and lift three times.
flow.say: Look at the hairs in the water. Now lift it out slowly. What changed? What do you notice? What do you wonder?
flow.kid: Hold the brush in water. Look at the hairs. Lift it out. What changed?
flow.parent: In water the hairs float apart, and water touches every hair. In air the wet hairs cling into one point. Water is now touching only the outside of the bundle. Let your child say this in their own words.
flow.context: In this step of the Paintbrush Gill, you compare a brush in water with the same brush lifted into air.

flow.do: 1. Explain that a gill is thousands of thin red plates, much finer than brush hairs. 2. Ask your child to draw what happens to them in air. 3. Keep the drawing for later.
flow.say: A gill is made of thousands of plates, finer than these hairs. Draw what you think happens to them when a fish is lifted out.
flow.kid: A gill has thousands of thin plates. Draw what happens to them in air. Keep your drawing.
flow.think: Your lungs are thin and wet inside too. Why do they not stick shut in air?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Paintbrush Gill. You draw what you think happens to a gill in air.

activities.title: The Bean Gill: does the direction of flow matter?
activities.context: In this activity paper cups stand for small amounts of water and blood passing each other in a gill, and beans stand for oxygen. You move the cups the same way, then opposite ways, and count how many beans the blood collects each time.

materials.item: 8 small cups, bowls or squares of paper: 4 marked W for water and 4 marked B for blood
about 100 dried beans, rajma, chana or tamarind seeds
a strip of floor or table about 1 metre long
a notebook and a pencil

activities.record: Write how many beans a blood cup carries away in the same-way test. Then write the number for each round of the opposite-way test. Under them, write which way collects more, and why you think so.

setup.art: Two paper cups side by side, one marked W holding 16 beans and one marked B holding none, with an arrow showing both moving the same way.
setup.caption: 1. Same way: a water cup with 16 beans travels beside an empty blood cup. At each stop they share equally.

setup.art: A row of four W cups above a row of four B cups, with an arrow pointing right over the W row and an arrow pointing left under the B row.
setup.caption: 2. Opposite ways: four water cups face four blood cups. Each facing pair shares equally.

setup.art: A child sliding the W row one place to the right and the B row one place to the left, with a full new W cup entering at the left and an empty new B cup entering at the right.
setup.caption: 3. Slide the water row right and the blood row left. Count the beans in the blood cup that leaves.

flow.do: 1. Put 16 beans in one W cup and none in one B cup. 2. Stand them side by side. 3. The sharing rule: beans move from the fuller cup until both are equal. 4. Share, move both cups one step along together, and share again, four times.
flow.say: Beans only move from the fuller cup to the emptier one. Share until they are equal. Now move on together. Does anything more happen?
flow.kid: Put 16 beans in W. Share until W and B are equal. Move both along. Share again.

ask.q: How many beans did the blood cup end with? Why did it stop there?
good: 8. After that the two cups were equal.
Nothing moves when both have the same.

flow.parent: After the first stop both cups hold 8, and nothing more moves. Travelling the same way, the blood can never collect more than half. If a pair holds an odd number, the water cup keeps the extra bean.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Bean Gill. Water and blood travel the same way, and you count what the blood collects.

flow.do: 1. Ask what will happen if blood and water move in opposite directions. 2. Ask for a number and a reason. 3. Write the guess down.
flow.say: Now the blood will travel against the water. Will a blood cup collect more than 8 beans, fewer, or the same? Why?
flow.kid: Now blood goes the other way. Will it collect more than 8 beans? Guess, and say why.
flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children say 'the same', because the same cups and beans are used.
flow.context: In this step of the Bean Gill, you guess what happens when blood travels against the water.

flow.do: 1. Lay 4 empty W cups in a row, and 4 empty B cups in a row facing them. 2. Each round: slide the W row one place right and the B row one place left. 3. A new W cup with 16 beans enters at the left. A new empty B cup enters at the right. 4. Each facing pair shares equally. 5. Count the beans in the B cup that slides out at the left. Play 10 rounds.
flow.say: Slide, bring in new cups, share, and count the blood cup that leaves. Write the number for every round.
flow.kid: Slide water right and blood left. Add new cups. Share. Count the blood cup that leaves.
flow.parent: Reuse the cups that slide out. Empty a used W cup before refilling it with 16. The leaving blood cup holds 0 in round 1, then 8, 8, 10, 10, 11, 11, 11, 11, and 12 by round 10. It then stays at 12. Each pair shares only if the water cup has more. The water cup keeps any odd bean.

check.q: In the Bean Gill, the blood cup about to leave holds 11 beans. Which water cup does it meet last?
check.why: Blood leaves at the end where fresh water comes in. So even a nearly full blood cup meets water with more beans, and beans still cross. If you chose the old cup, look again at which end the new water enters.

flow.context: In this step of the Bean Gill, water and blood travel opposite ways, and you count what the blood collects in each round.

flow.do: 1. Put the two results side by side: 8 of 16, and about 12 of 16. 2. Ask your child why the opposite way collects more. 3. Look at the beans left in the water cup that slides out.
flow.say: Same cups, same beans, same rule. Only the direction changed. Why did the blood collect more this time?
flow.kid: Compare your two results. Only the direction changed. Why did the blood collect more?
flow.think: A real gill has far more than 4 stops. Would more stops let the blood collect even more than 12 of 16?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Bean Gill. You compare the two ways and explain the difference.

activities.title: Find a Valve in a Vein: William Harvey's finger test
activities.context: In this activity you find a one-way valve in a vein on the back of a hand. The doctor William Harvey used this test in 1628 to show that blood in veins moves only towards the heart.

materials.item: a grown-up's hand with veins that show on the back. A grandparent's hand is often best
a notebook and a pencil

activities.safety: Press gently with a fingertip only. Do not tie anything round an arm.
activities.record: Draw the back of the hand and the vein you tested. Mark where each finger pressed. Draw an arrow for the direction the blood was moving, and write how you know. Also write what you felt at your wrist, and how it was different from the vein.

setup.art: An older woman's hand hanging down beside her chair, with the veins on the back of the hand standing out.
setup.caption: 1. Let the hand hang down for a minute, until the veins stand out.

setup.art: A child's fingertip pressing on one vein near the knuckles of the older woman's hand, which now rests on a table.
setup.caption: 2. Press one fingertip on a vein, near the knuckles.

setup.art: A second child's finger sliding along the same vein towards the wrist while the first finger stays pressed, leaving the vein flat between them.
setup.caption: 3. With another finger, stroke the vein towards the wrist. Lift the second finger. Does the vein fill?

setup.art: A child pressing two fingertips on the thumb side of her own wrist, with a small heart and wavy lines to show the beats.
setup.caption: 4. Feel your own pulse at the wrist. This is an artery.

flow.do: 1. Ask the grown-up to let one hand hang down for a minute. 2. Rest the hand on a table. 3. Choose a long, straight vein on the back. 4. Ask which way the blood in it is moving, and how we could find out.
flow.say: The blood in this vein is moving. Which way, towards the fingers or towards the heart? How could we find out without looking inside?
flow.kid: Find a vein on the back of the hand. Which way is the blood moving? Guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of Find a Valve in a Vein. You guess which way the blood in a vein is moving.

flow.do: 1. Press one fingertip on the vein near the knuckles and keep it there. 2. With another finger, stroke along the vein towards the wrist, pushing the blood out. 3. Lift the second finger. 4. Watch whether the empty part fills from the wrist end.
flow.say: My first finger stops new blood coming from the fingers. I have pushed the blood out. Will the vein fill back from the wrist end?
flow.kid: Press one finger near the knuckles. Stroke the vein towards the wrist. Lift that finger and watch.
flow.parent: The vein usually stays flat up to a certain point, which is a valve. Blood beyond the valve does not flow back. When you lift the first finger, the vein fills at once from the finger end. If it fills from the wrist end, you stroked past a place where another vein joins. Try a different stretch.
flow.context: In this step of Find a Valve in a Vein, you empty a stretch of vein and see from which end it fills.

flow.do: 1. Lift the first finger and watch the vein fill. 2. Ask what this shows about the direction of the blood. 3. Ask what must be inside the vein to stop it flowing back.
flow.say: It filled only when I lifted the finger near the knuckles. So which way does blood move in this vein? What stops it going back?
flow.kid: Lift the first finger. Watch the vein fill. Which way does the blood move?

check.q: A vein in the hand stays empty until the finger nearer the fingertips is lifted. What does this show?
options: Blood in it flows towards the fingers
Blood in it flows towards the heart
check.why: The vein filled only from the finger end, so blood enters from there and moves towards the wrist and the heart. Valves stop it from flowing back. If you chose 'towards the fingers', the vein would have filled from the wrist end.

flow.context: This is the last step of Find a Valve in a Vein. You work out which way the blood moves and what stops it going back.

flow.do: 1. Hold out your own hand, palm up. 2. Lay two fingertips, not your thumb, on the thumb side of the wrist. 3. Press gently until you feel a tap. 4. Count the taps for 15 seconds. 5. Now touch a vein on the back of your hand. Do you feel taps there?
flow.say: This tapping is your pulse. It is a different kind of vessel from the vein we just tested. Do you feel taps in the vein?
flow.kid: Find the tapping on your wrist with two fingers. Count the taps. Then touch a vein on the back of your hand. Is it tapping too?
flow.parent: The tapping is an artery swelling each time the left ventricle pushes blood out. Arteries carry blood away from the heart, in beats. A vein has no beat, because the push is gone by the time blood reaches it. Do not press hard, and do not press on the neck.
flow.context: This step of Find a Valve in a Vein compares an artery with a vein. Here you feel your pulse at the wrist.

activities.title: Three Hearts on Paper: draw the loops of a fish, a frog and a human
activities.context: In this activity you draw the path of the blood in three animals, with a red pencil for blood that is rich in oxygen and a blue pencil for blood that has given oxygen up. A drawing like this is a model. It explains what you cannot see.

materials.item: 3 sheets of paper
a red pencil, a blue pencil and an ordinary pencil

activities.record: Keep the three drawings. Under each, write the number of chambers, the number of loops, and the places where red and blue blood meet or mix.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with three boxes drawn in a line and labelled heart, gills and body, joined into one loop by arrows.
setup.caption: 1. Fish: draw one loop. Heart, then gills, then body, then back to the heart.

setup.art: A sheet with a heart of three chambers in the middle, a small loop to boxes labelled lungs and skin, and a large loop to a box labelled body.
setup.caption: 2. Frog: draw two loops that meet in one ventricle.

setup.art: A sheet with a heart of four chambers, a small loop to the lungs coloured blue then red, and a large loop to the body coloured red then blue.
setup.caption: 3. Human: draw two loops that never mix. Colour all three in red and blue.

flow.do: 1. On the first sheet, draw a heart with two chambers, one behind the other. 2. Draw the gills and the body. 3. Join them into one loop with arrows. 4. Colour the blood blue until the gills and red after them.
flow.say: A fish's blood goes from the heart to the gills, and straight on to the body. Where does the colour change? Where is the push strongest?
flow.kid: Draw a fish heart, gills and body in one loop. Colour blue before the gills and red after.
flow.parent: The whole fish heart holds blue blood, which has given up its oxygen. The push is strongest just after the heart and weakest after the body.
flow.context: This is the first step of Three Hearts on Paper. You draw the single loop of a fish.

flow.do: 1. On the second sheet, draw a heart with two atria above one ventricle. 2. Draw one loop to the lungs and skin and back to the left atrium. 3. Draw one loop to the body and back to the right atrium. 4. Ask what colour the ventricle should be.
flow.say: Red blood and blue blood both pour into one ventricle. What colour will you make it? What goes out to the body?
flow.kid: Draw a frog heart with three chambers and two loops. What colour is the one ventricle?

ask.q: What colour did you make the ventricle, and why?
good: Purple, because the two bloods partly mix.
Red on one side and blue on the other, with a mixed part.

flow.parent: Purple, or red and blue side by side, are both good answers. Folds inside the frog's ventricle keep the two streams partly apart, so the mixing is not complete.
flow.context: In this step of Three Hearts on Paper, you draw the two loops of a frog, which meet in one ventricle.

flow.do: 1. On the third sheet, draw a heart with four chambers. 2. Draw the small loop: right ventricle, lungs, left atrium. 3. Draw the large loop: left ventricle, body, right atrium. 4. Colour them, and compare all three sheets.
flow.say: Follow one drop of blood with your finger all the way round. How many times does it pass through the heart on one trip?
flow.kid: Draw a human heart with four chambers and two loops. Follow one drop round with your finger.

check.q: In a human, which chamber pumps blood that is rich in oxygen out to the body?
check.why: Blood comes back from the lungs to the left atrium and passes into the left ventricle, which pumps it to the body. The right ventricle pumps blood to the lungs. If you chose the right ventricle, trace the small loop again on your drawing.

flow.think: Before you were born, your lungs were full of liquid and your oxygen came through a cord. Where do you think your blood went then?
flow.context: This is the last step of Three Hearts on Paper. You draw the two separate loops of a human and compare the three plans.

activities.title: The One-Way Pipe: how much clean water clears a tube?
activities.context: In the Half-Breath Test, a tumbler with one opening needed many pours to clear. In this activity you clear a tube that is open at both ends, as a fish's gill chamber is. You count how much clean water it needs.

materials.item: a clear tube open at both ends: a clear straw, a short piece of clear aquarium tubing, or the empty barrel of a clear ball pen
a medicine dropper, an ink filler or a syringe without a needle. A second straw, used with a finger over the top, also works
a small cup of dark water, such as strong black tea, and a tumbler of clean water
a bowl and a sheet of white paper

activities.record: Write how many dropper-fuls of dark water filled the tube, and how many dropper-fuls of clean water cleared it. Beside these, write your counts from the Half-Breath Test.

setup.art: A clear straw held at a gentle slope over a bowl, full of dark brown water, with white paper behind it.
setup.caption: 1. Fill the tube with dark water, counting the dropper-fuls. Hold it at a gentle slope over a bowl.

setup.art: A dropper adding clean water to the upper end of the sloping straw, with dark water running out of the lower end into the bowl.
setup.caption: 2. Add clean water at the top end, one dropper-ful at a time.

setup.art: The same straw now clear along its whole length, and a child holding up fingers to show the count.
setup.caption: 3. Count the dropper-fuls until the whole tube is clear.

flow.do: 1. Hold the tube at a gentle slope over the bowl, with a finger under the low end. 2. Fill it with dark water, counting the dropper-fuls. 3. Ask how many dropper-fuls of clean water will clear it. 4. Ask for the reason.
flow.say: This tube took this many dropper-fuls to fill. How many dropper-fuls of clean water will make it clear? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Fill the tube with dark water. Count the dropper-fuls. Guess how many will clear it.
flow.parent: Remind your child that the tumbler needed several times its own volume of clean water. Many children now expect the same of the tube.
flow.context: This is the first step of the One-Way Pipe. You fill a tube with dark water and guess how much clean water will clear it.

flow.do: 1. Take the finger away from the low end. 2. Add clean water at the top end, one dropper-ful at a time. 3. Watch the dark water leave at the low end. 4. Count until the whole tube looks clear against the white paper.
flow.say: Watch where the dark water goes. Does the clean water mix with it, or push it along?
flow.kid: Add clean water at the top. Watch the dark water leave. Count until the tube is clear.
flow.parent: The clean water mostly pushes the dark water ahead of it. The tube is usually clear after one to three times the amount that filled it. A little colour clings to the wall, so it is not exactly once.
flow.context: In this step of the One-Way Pipe, you push clean water through the tube from one end and count how much it takes.

flow.do: 1. Put the tube result beside the tumbler result from the Half-Breath Test. 2. Ask why the tube cleared with so much less water. 3. Ask which is like a lung and which is like a gill.
flow.say: The tumbler needed about seven half-fills. The tube needed far less. What is different about the way the water moves?
flow.kid: Compare the tube with the tumbler. Why did the tube clear so quickly? Which is like a gill?

check.q: Why does a tube open at both ends clear with less water than a tumbler with one opening?
options: The tube is made of plastic
Old water leaves before it can mix
check.why: In the tube, new water pushes old water out at the far end. In the tumbler, new water is stirred into old, and each pour throws away some of the new water too. If you chose 'plastic', try a glass tube or a steel pipe in your mind. The flow would be the same.

flow.context: This is the last step of the One-Way Pipe. You compare flow through a tube with flow in and out of a tumbler.

activities.title: The Price of Lungs: catch the water in your breath
activities.context: The inside of a lung must be wet, because oxygen has to dissolve in water before it can cross into the blood. In this activity you see what that costs a body that breathes air, and you test whether the nose gives back some of the water.

materials.item: a steel plate or a small mirror, cooled for 10 minutes in the fridge
a ruler
a clock or phone that shows seconds
a notebook and a pencil

activities.record: Draw the fog patches from the mouth breath and from the nose breath, with their widths. Write how many seconds each took to vanish. Write what you think the patches are made of.

setup.art: A child holding a cold steel plate upright a hand's width from her open mouth and breathing out onto it, leaving a round fog patch.
setup.caption: 1. Breathe out slowly through your mouth onto a cold plate. Measure the fog patch.

setup.art: The same child with her mouth closed, breathing out through her nose onto the plate held just under it, leaving two small fog patches.
setup.caption: 2. Wipe the plate. Breathe out through your nose. Measure again.

setup.art: A child watching a fog patch shrink on a steel plate with a phone timer beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Time how long each patch takes to vanish.

flow.do: 1. Take the plate from the fridge and wipe it dry. 2. Ask what will appear on it when your child breathes out onto it, and where that comes from. 3. Ask whether mouth breath and nose breath will be the same.
flow.say: What will your breath leave on this cold plate? Where does that come from? Will your nose and your mouth leave the same amount?
flow.kid: Wipe the cold plate. What will your breath leave on it? Guess, and say why.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Price of Lungs. You guess what your breath will leave on a cold plate.

flow.do: 1. Hold the plate a hand's width from the mouth. 2. Breathe out slowly once, for a count of three. 3. Measure the patch and time how long it lasts. 4. Wipe the plate, and repeat with one slow breath out through the nose.
flow.say: One slow breath for a count of three, the same each time. Measure the patch, and time it until it is gone.
flow.kid: Breathe out slowly onto the plate. Measure the patch. Time it. Then try your nose.
flow.parent: The fog is tiny drops of water. The mouth patch is usually larger and lasts longer than the two nose patches. If the plate warms up, cool it again, because a warm plate does not fog. Write what you really see.
flow.context: In this step of the Price of Lungs, you compare the fog from a mouth breath with the fog from a nose breath.

flow.do: 1. Ask where the water came from. 2. Ask why the nose might leave less. 3. After your child has answered, read the note below aloud.
flow.say: Where did this water come from? Why might the nose patch be smaller? Say what you think first.
flow.kid: Where did the water come from? Why is the nose patch smaller? Say what you think.

ask.q: Why must the inside of a lung be wet?
good: Oxygen has to dissolve in water before it can cross.
A dry surface would not let oxygen through.

flow.parent: The note to read: the air you breathe out has passed over the wet lining of your lungs, so it carries water away. An adult loses about a third of a litre of water a day like this. Air going out through the nose is cooled a little on the way, and some of the water stays behind on the lining of the nose. A smaller stream of air also makes a smaller patch, so this test alone cannot say how much the nose saves.
flow.think: A fish's gills are in water all the time. A camel breathes very dry air. Which of them needs a nose that saves water?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Price of Lungs. You say where the water in your breath came from and why the nose leaves less.

projects.title: The Breather Survey: how do the animals round you move air or water?
projects.context: In this three-day project you watch at least ten animals, including people, and record what moves when each one breathes. You sort them by how they get oxygen, and you make a chart of how fast they breathe.

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil
a clock or phone that shows seconds
a large sheet of chart paper and colour pencils
a hand lens, if you have one

projects.safety: Watch every animal from where they are, and do not catch, hold or chase anyone. Stay away from stray dogs, wasps' nests and deep water. A grown-up comes along to the market or the pond.

schedule.what: Write the question and your guesses. Watch the animals at home: people, a pet, a house gecko, an ant, a fly. Record what moves when each one breathes.
Go to a fish stall, an aquarium shop, a pond or a park with a grown-up. Watch fish, birds and insects. Count breaths where you can.
Sort your animals by how they get oxygen. Draw a bar chart of breaths in one minute. Write what you found and what you could not see.

projects.record: A table with one row for each animal, a poster that sorts the animals by how they get oxygen, and a bar chart of breaths in one minute. End with one thing the survey could not show.

setup.art: A notebook table with columns headed animal, what moves, breaths in one minute, air or water, and how they get oxygen.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a table with five columns.

setup.art: A child crouching a little way from a crow on a wall, watching the bird's tail bob, with a phone timer in her hand.
setup.caption: 2. Watch each animal quietly. What moves when they breathe? Count for one minute if you can.

setup.art: A chart-paper poster with four groups labelled lungs, gills, air tubes and skin, with small drawings of animals in each.
setup.caption: 3. Sort your animals into groups on a poster.

flow.do: 1. Day 1. Write the question: what moves when different animals breathe? 2. Ask for a guess about a gecko, an ant and a fish. 3. Draw the table. 4. Watch four or five animals at home, starting with a sleeping person.
flow.say: On a person, the chest and belly move. What do you think moves on a gecko? On an ant? On a fish? Why?
flow.kid: Write your question and your guesses. Draw the table. Watch the animals at home.

ask.q: Why might you see nothing move on an ant?
good: An ant is too small for me to see anything move.
Air may get in without the ant pumping.
Ants use air tubes, not a chest.

flow.parent: A house gecko's sides and throat move quickly. A sleeping adult takes about 12 to 18 breaths a minute, and a child a few more. Nothing can be seen moving on an ant. 'Could not see' is a real result, so write it down.
flow.context: This is day 1 of the Breather Survey. You write your guesses and watch the animals at home.

flow.do: 1. Day 2. Visit a fish stall, an aquarium shop, a pond or a park. 2. Watch a live fish and count the beats of the gill cover for one minute. 3. Watch a crow or a pigeon at rest, and a large insect if you find one. 4. Fill in the table.
flow.say: Watch the mouth and the gill cover of the fish. Do they open together or in turn? Now count the gill cover for one minute.
flow.kid: Watch a fish. Count the gill cover beats for one minute. Watch a bird and an insect too.
flow.parent: The fish's mouth and gill covers open in turn, which pumps water one way. Fish in a crowded or warm tank beat faster. A resting bird's tail or back bobs gently. On a grasshopper, a wasp or a dragonfly, look for the abdomen pulsing. If there are no live fish near you, use a short video of a fish in a tank.
flow.context: This is day 2 of the Breather Survey. You watch fish, birds and insects outside your home.

flow.do: 1. Day 3. Sort the animals on a poster: lungs, gills, air tubes, skin. 2. Draw a bar chart of breaths in one minute for the animals you could count. 3. Write what you found. 4. Write one thing the survey could not show.
flow.say: Which animals breathed fastest? Were they the small ones or the large ones? What could you not find out by watching?
flow.kid: Sort your animals on a poster. Draw a bar chart of breaths. Write what you found.

ask.q: What could this survey not show?
good: What happens inside, such as the heart and the blood.
Whether the animal was resting or frightened.
How ants and other small insects move air.

flow.parent: Smaller animals with lungs usually breathe faster than larger ones. An animal who is being watched may be alarmed and breathe faster, and that is a fair limit to write down.
flow.context: This is day 3 of the Breather Survey. You sort your animals, chart their breathing and say what watching cannot show.

challenges.title: A Gill for Dry Land: pack wet surface into a matchbox without letting it stick
challenges.context: A gill fails in air because its wet plates cling together. A lung has the same problem and solves it. This is a design challenge. You pack as much wet paper surface as you can into a matchbox, with air touching both sides of every piece.
challenges.problem: Fit as much thin paper as you can into the tray of a matchbox. Then wet it. Air must still be able to reach both sides of every piece of paper. Paper that is stuck to other paper does not count.
constraints: Everything must fit inside one matchbox tray.
The paper is dipped in water for two seconds before it is judged.
Only paper with air on both sides is counted.
You may use spacers, but they must also fit in the tray.
materials: thin paper, such as newspaper or tissue wrapping paper
toothpicks, broom-stick pieces or matchsticks without heads, for spacers
general: Cut strips as wide as the tray is deep. Stand them on edge in rows, like the pages of a book standing open.
Fold one long strip back and forth into pleats, like a paper fan, so that each fold holds the next one away.
Put a toothpick between each pair of sheets to keep a gap.
creative: Roll a strip into a loose spiral with a thread wound along it as a spacer. The air tubes of insects are held open by a stiff spiral thread in their walls.
Make many small paper tubes and stand them side by side, like a honeycomb. A tube holds itself open when it is wet. Alveoli are small, rounded sacs for a similar reason.

Rub a little soap solution on the paper before wetting it and see whether the wet sheets peel apart more easily. Your alveoli are lined with a soap-like liquid called surfactant. In 1959 the doctor Mary Ellen Avery showed that babies born too early struggle to breathe because they do not yet make enough of it.
challenges.your_turn: Change one thing in your design so that more paper stays apart when wet. Say what you changed and why you expected it to work. Wet it again, measure, and say what happened.

setup.art: An empty matchbox tray beside strips of newspaper, toothpicks, thread and scissors on a table.
setup.caption: 1. Plan how to pack paper into the tray so that the pieces do not touch.

setup.art: A matchbox tray filled with pleated paper strips standing on edge, with toothpicks between some of them, being lowered into a bowl of water.
setup.caption: 2. Build it. Dip it in water for two seconds and lift it out.

setup.art: A child gently pulling wet paper strips out of the tray and laying the ones that stayed separate along a ruler.
setup.caption: 3. Take out only the paper that still has air on both sides. Measure its total length.

flow.do: 1. Read the problem and the rules together. 2. Wet two small pieces of paper and press them together, to feel how they cling. 3. Ask how your child will keep wet sheets apart. 4. Ask them to sketch a plan.
flow.say: Feel how wet paper clings. Your design must stop that. What will hold the sheets apart? Draw your plan first.
flow.kid: Feel how wet paper sticks. Plan how to keep the sheets apart. Draw your plan.

ask.q: Why do wet sheets cling when dry sheets do not?
good: The water between them pulls them together.
Water sticks to both sheets at once.

flow.parent: Let your child try their own idea first, even if you expect it to fail. A first design that collapses when wet teaches more than one that is copied.
flow.context: This is the first step of A Gill for Dry Land. You plan how to pack paper into a matchbox so that it stays apart when wet.

flow.do: 1. Cut the paper and build the design in the tray. 2. Measure the total length of paper strip used, and write it down. 3. Dip the tray in water for two seconds. 4. Lift it out and look closely at which pieces have stuck.
flow.say: Write down how much paper went in. Now dip it. Look closely. Which pieces still have air on both sides?
flow.kid: Build your design. Measure the paper you used. Dip it in water. Which pieces stuck?
flow.parent: A grown-up helps with the scissors. To score, pull out only the strips that are not stuck to a neighbour, and measure their total length. Length is a fair measure because every strip has the same width.

check.q: A child packs 60 centimetres of paper strip into a matchbox. After wetting, 20 centimetres still have air on both sides. What is the score?
check.why: Only paper that air can reach on both sides can do the work of a breathing surface. The 40 centimetres that stuck together are like gill plates clumped in air. If you chose 60, you counted the paper that went in, not the paper that still works.

flow.context: In this step of A Gill for Dry Land, you build your design, wet it and count the paper that stayed apart.

flow.do: 1. Change one thing to keep more paper apart. 2. Build, wet and measure again. 3. Compare the two scores. 4. Ask how a real lung keeps its wet walls from sticking.
flow.say: Change one thing and test again. Did the score go up? How do you think a real lung stops its wet walls from sticking?
flow.kid: Change one thing. Wet it and measure again. Did more paper stay apart?
flow.think: More paper means more surface, but less room for air to move between the sheets. Where is the best balance?
flow.context: This is the last step of A Gill for Dry Land. You improve your design and compare it with a real lung.

challenges.title: Carry the Fish Home: keep four fish breathing for two hours with no pump
challenges.context: Fish sellers and fish farmers have to move live fish in hot weather. The fish use up the oxygen dissolved in the water. This is a design challenge on paper, with one real measurement. You plan how to carry four small fish for two hours with no electric pump.
challenges.problem: Plan a way to carry four small live fish for two hours on a hot day, by bus or scooter, with no electric air pump. The fish must have enough oxygen for the whole trip.
constraints: You may use only 2 litres of water, because water is heavy.
The container must not spill on a bumpy road.
Nothing in your plan may hurt the fish.
materials: paper and a pencil for the plan
three containers of different shapes that each hold 1 litre: a bottle, a pot and a wide basin or tray
general: Use a wide container. Oxygen enters water only through the surface that touches air, so a wider surface lets more in.
Keep the water cool with shade and a wet cloth. Cool water holds more oxygen, and cool fish use less.
Fill a strong bag one third with water and two thirds with air, and tie it shut. Pet shops pack fish this way.
creative: Keep the water moving. In the old way of carrying young fish in Bengal, carriers kept shaking the earthen pots as they walked, so that air mixed into the water.
Fill the space in the bag with oxygen from a cylinder, in place of air. Fish farms across India send young fish by road and rail in bags packed like this.
Choose the fish. A murrel or a climbing perch can gulp air at the surface. Sellers carry them alive in very little water, as long as they stay damp.
challenges.your_turn: Choose one container and one extra idea for your plan. Say why your fish will have enough oxygen at the end of two hours. Then say what could still go wrong.

setup.art: A bottle, a round pot and a wide basin in a row, each holding one litre of water, with a child measuring across the top of the water in each.
setup.caption: 1. Pour 1 litre into each container. Measure how wide the water surface is.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with a child's labelled drawing of a wide covered tub wrapped in a wet cloth, with four small fish inside.
setup.caption: 2. Draw your plan. Label what brings oxygen in and what keeps the water cool.

setup.art: A clear plastic bag one third full of water with four small fish, the top blown up with air and tied with a rubber band.
setup.caption: 3. Compare your plan with the way a pet shop packs fish.

flow.do: 1. Read the problem and the rules together. 2. Ask where the oxygen in the water comes from, and where it goes. 3. Ask what will happen to it during two hours. 4. List ideas without judging them.
flow.say: Four fish are using up the oxygen in the water. How can more oxygen get in during the trip? Tell me every idea you have.
flow.kid: Read the problem. Where does oxygen in water come from? List your ideas.

ask.q: How does oxygen get into water?
good: From the air, through the surface.
Splashing and stirring mix more air in.
Water plants make it in the light.

flow.parent: Accept every idea at this stage. If your child suggests filling the container to the brim to stop spills, ask how air will then reach the water.
flow.context: This is the first step of Carry the Fish Home. You think about how oxygen gets into water and list ideas.

flow.do: 1. Pour 1 litre of water into each of the three containers. 2. Measure the width of the water surface in each. 3. Ask which lets in the most oxygen, and why. 4. Stand each on newspaper and shake it gently, to see which spills.
flow.say: Each holds the same litre. Which has the biggest surface touching the air? Which would spill on a bumpy road?
flow.kid: Pour 1 litre into each container. Measure across the water. Which surface is widest?
flow.parent: The basin has the widest surface and spills most easily. The bottle hardly spills and has the smallest surface. A good design has to balance the two, and that is the real problem fish carriers face.

check.q: One litre of water is put in a narrow bottle and one litre in a wide basin. Which takes in oxygen from the air faster?
options: The bottle, because it is deeper
Both the same, because both hold 1 litre
The basin, with the wider surface
check.why: Oxygen enters water only where water touches air. The basin has far more of that surface. If you chose 'both the same', you were thinking of how much water there is. That decides how much oxygen the water starts with, not how fast more can get in.

flow.context: In this step of Carry the Fish Home, you measure the water surface of three containers that hold the same amount.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to draw the final plan and label it. 2. Ask them to explain how oxygen gets in and how the water stays cool. 3. Read the usual and creative solutions together. 4. Ask what they would now change.
flow.say: Show me your plan. How does oxygen get in? How does the water stay cool? What could still go wrong?
flow.kid: Draw your plan and label it. Say how oxygen gets in. What could go wrong?
flow.think: Fish farmers often stop feeding fish a day before a journey. Why might a fish with an empty gut need less oxygen and keep the water cleaner?
flow.context: This is the last step of Carry the Fish Home. You draw your final plan and compare it with real ways of carrying fish.

items.p: Where does oxygen pass from the air into your blood?
items.why: The alveoli are the tiny air sacs at the ends of the airways. Their walls are thin enough for oxygen to diffuse through. The trachea and nose only carry the air.

items.p: What happens to the air in your lungs during one quiet breath?
items.why: A quiet breath brings in a small amount of new air, which mixes with the air that stayed in the lungs. If you chose 'all of it', remember that the lungs never empty.

items.p: Why do gills stop working in air?
opts: Air is too light to pump
items.why: In water each thin plate floats free. In air the wet plates stick to each other, and most of the surface is lost. Air has plenty of oxygen.

items.p: How many chambers does a fish's heart have?
items.why: A fish's heart has one atrium and one ventricle. It pumps blood to the gills, and the blood goes straight on to the body.

items.p: Which of these animals has an open circulatory system?
items.why: A grasshopper's tube heart pumps haemolymph into the spaces of the body. The earthworm, the fish and the crow keep their blood inside vessels.

items.p: After you breathe out as hard as you can, your lungs are empty.
items.why: False. About a litre of air stays in an adult's lungs even after the hardest breath out. It is called residual air.

items.p: A plant takes in oxygen only in the dark.
items.why: False. Plant cells need oxygen day and night. In sunlight a leaf also makes oxygen, more than the plant uses, so the plant gives out extra oxygen.

items.p: Water flows over a fish's gills in one direction only.
items.why: True. Water comes in at the mouth and leaves behind the gill cover. It does not turn round, as the air in your lungs does.

items.p: The sheet of muscle under your lungs that pulls air in is the ____.
items.why: When the diaphragm tightens it moves down, the chest gets bigger, and air flows in.

items.p: The small openings along an insect's sides that let air in are called ____.
items.why: Air goes in through the spiracles and along the air tubes, the tracheae, to the cells.

items.p: Short hairs inside the nose catch big bits of ____ before the air goes on.
items.why: The hairs catch the bigger bits of dust, and mucus and cilia deal with the finer dust further down.

items.p: Match each animal to what they breathe with.
items.why: Each of these is a thin, wet surface where oxygen can cross. They differ in where the surface is and how air or water is brought to it.

items.p: Put the path of air into your lungs in order, starting from outside.
items.why: Air enters at the nose, goes down the trachea, divides into the two bronchi and ends in the alveoli.

items.p: Sort each animal by kind of circulatory system.
items.why: In crabs, cockroaches and snails, the liquid leaves the vessels and washes round the organs. In humans, octopuses and earthworms, the blood stays inside vessels.

items.p: Match each blood vessel to what it does.
pairs: carries blood away from the heart, with a beat
carries blood back to the heart, with valves inside
the thinnest vessel, where oxygen passes to the cells
items.why: The names tell the direction, not the oxygen. The pulmonary artery is an artery, though its blood is low in oxygen.

items.p: Air holds more oxygen than water. Explain why a fish still suffocates in air.
items.a: A gill is made of very thin, wet plates. In water they float apart, and water touches every plate. In air they cling together and dry, so there is very little surface left for oxygen to cross.
items.why: A strong answer says that the surface is lost. It does not say that air lacks oxygen or has the wrong kind.

items.p: In the Half-Breath Test, why did two half-breaths not clear the tumbler?
items.a: The first breath left half of the dark water. The clean water mixed with it. The second pour took out half of the mixture, so a quarter of the dark water was still there.
items.why: A strong answer says that the new water mixes with the old before the next pour, so each pour removes clean water as well as dark.

items.p: Draw the path of a fish's blood as one loop. Label the heart, the gills and the body.
items.a: One loop with arrows: heart, then gills, then body, then back to the heart. The blood is low in oxygen from the body to the gills, and rich in oxygen from the gills to the body.
items.why: A strong drawing has a single loop, with the gills between the heart and the body. The blood passes through the heart once on each trip.
items.art: A blank outline of a fish seen from the side, with space inside to draw the heart, the gills and a loop.

items.p: About how much of the air deep in an adult's lungs does one quiet breath change?
items.why: About 350 millilitres of new air reaches the alveoli and mixes with roughly 2 litres already there. That is about one part in seven.

items.p: In a gill, why does blood flow against the water and not with it?
opts: So oxygen keeps crossing all along
items.why: Flowing against the water, the blood always meets water with a little more oxygen than the blood has. So oxygen crosses along the whole length.

items.p: Which side of your heart pushes harder, and where does it send blood?
items.why: The left ventricle sends blood to the whole body at high pressure. The right ventricle sends blood only to the lungs, gently.

items.p: What carries oxygen to the cells of a grasshopper?
items.why: Tracheae carry air from the spiracles right to the cells. The haemolymph of a grasshopper carries almost no oxygen.

items.p: What happens to the watery liquid that leaks out of your capillaries?
opts: It is all lost as sweat
It collects in the feet for good
It turns into red blood cells
Lymph vessels return it to the blood
items.why: Most of the liquid goes back into the capillaries. The rest, about 3 litres a day in an adult, is collected by lymph vessels and returned near the heart.

items.p: Air flows one way through a bird's lungs, on the breath in and on the breath out.
items.why: True. Air sacs work as bellows and push air through the stiff lungs in the same direction in both halves of the breath.

items.p: A frog's heart keeps blood from the lungs and blood from the body fully apart.
items.why: False. A frog has one ventricle, and the two kinds of blood partly mix in it. A human ventricle is divided in two.

items.p: The copper protein that makes an octopus's blood blue is called ____.
items.why: Haemocyanin carries oxygen with copper. Our haemoglobin carries it with iron and is red.

items.p: Match each animal to their heart.
items.why: The fish has one loop and two chambers. The frog has two loops that meet in one ventricle. The crow has two separate loops. The octopus has one heart for each gill and one for the body.

items.p: Every artery carries blood that is full of oxygen.
items.why: False. The pulmonary artery carries blood from the heart to the lungs, and that blood is low in oxygen. An artery is named by its direction, away from the heart.

items.p: A drop of blood leaves your right ventricle. Put the next four places in order.
items.why: The right ventricle pumps blood to the lungs. It returns to the left atrium, passes into the left ventricle and is pumped to the body.

items.p: In the Bean Gill, water starts with 16 beans. Moving the same way, how many can blood collect at most?
items.why: The two cups share until they are equal, at 8 each. After that nothing moves, because beans only go from the fuller cup to the emptier one.

items.p: Three of these animals keep their blood inside vessels. Which is the odd one out?
items.why: A snail has an open circulatory system. The earthworm, the octopus and the fish have closed ones.

items.p: Explain why a second pump helps an animal with lungs. Use the word 'pressure'.
items.a: Blood loses pressure when it is pushed through the tiny capillaries of the lungs. The second pump, the left ventricle, gives it high pressure again so that it can reach the whole body. The lungs can then be kept at a gentle pressure.
items.why: A strong answer says that pressure is lost in the lung capillaries and given back by the left ventricle. A very strong answer adds that thin lung capillaries need a gentle push.

items.p: Fat builds up inside a grandfather's artery. Explain how this can cause a heart attack, and name two warning signs.
items.a: Fat narrows the artery, and a clot can block it. The heart muscle beyond the block gets no oxygen and starts to die. Warning signs are chest pain that spreads to the left arm, and sweating.
items.why: A strong answer links the blocked artery to the heart muscle's need for oxygen, and names two real signs.

items.p: Label the four chambers of this human heart.
a: Right atrium: receives blood from the body
Right ventricle: pumps blood to the lungs
Left atrium: receives blood from the lungs
Left ventricle: pumps blood to the body, and has the thickest wall
items.why: A heart is drawn as if the person is facing you, so the person's right side is on your left. The left ventricle has the thickest wall because it pushes hardest.
items.art: A simple front view of a human heart with four chambers, the lower left one drawn with a thicker wall, and four blank label lines.

items.p: Is a four-chambered heart better than a two-chambered heart?

views.says: Yes. Four chambers give the blood a second push, so it reaches the body fast and at high pressure.
No. A fish's heart is enough for a fish. The water holds the body up, and a second pump would cost extra food.
It depends on the life the animal leads. A four-chambered heart suits a warm, busy body on land.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give one reason from this lesson. Then say one thing that is right in another view.
items.a: Any view with a reason from the unit. For example: blood loses its push in the gills, which matters little to a fish in water. But a bird could not fly over mountains with a single loop.
items.why: Each view has something right. A strong answer names what the second pump gives and what it costs, and says for whom.

items.p: The voice box at the top of the trachea is called the ____.
items.why: Air passes through the larynx on the way to the trachea, and the vocal cords inside it make sound.

items.p: Lungs that mix old air with new waste part of each breath. What do they gain?
opts: More oxygen than a gill takes
A steady mixture for the blood
items.why: Because each breath changes only a little of the air, the oxygen and carbon dioxide next to the blood stay almost steady from breath to breath.

items.p: What helps an icefish live with no haemoglobin?
opts: Very cold water holds more oxygen
items.why: Cold water holds more dissolved oxygen, and a cold body uses less. An icefish also has a large heart that moves a great deal of blood.

items.p: An animal has air tubes that reach every cell. What might the blood not need to carry?
items.why: If air is piped straight to the cells, the blood is not needed for oxygen. It still has to carry food, waste and hormones.

items.p: In the Squirt Test, what stood for the capillaries of a gill?
items.why: Water had to push through thousands of tiny gaps in the cotton wool, as blood pushes through tiny capillaries. The bottle stood for the ventricle.

items.p: Oxygen pressure is higher in lung air than in the blood arriving. Which way does oxygen diffuse?
items.why: Diffusion goes from where there is more to where there is less. No pumping is needed. Carbon dioxide diffuses the other way for the same reason.

items.p: In an open circulatory system, the blood and the liquid round the cells are one liquid.
items.why: True. The liquid is called haemolymph. It leaves the vessels and washes over the organs directly.

items.p: The air you breathe out has no oxygen left in it.
items.why: False. Breathed-out air still has about 16 parts of oxygen in 100. Room air has about 21. That is why rescue breathing can help a person.

items.p: Blood and water flowing in opposite directions across a thin wall is called ____ exchange.
items.why: Counter-flow, or countercurrent, exchange lets the blood collect most of the oxygen from the water.

items.p: Sort each breathing organ by how the air or water moves through it.
cats: In and out the same way
items: In and out the same way
In and out the same way
In and out the same way
items.why: The lungs of mammals and frogs are bags with one opening. Water passes through gills from mouth to gill opening, and air sacs push air through a bird's lungs in one direction.

items.p: A tumbler is cleared by half-breaths. After 3 half-breaths, the old water left is one part in how many?
items.why: Each half-breath leaves half of what was there. Half of a half is a quarter, and half of a quarter is an eighth. So one part in 8 is left.

items.p: Three of these animals carry oxygen in their blood. Which is the odd one out?
items.why: A cockroach's haemolymph carries almost no oxygen, because air tubes take oxygen to the cells. The other three carry oxygen with haemoglobin or haemocyanin.

items.p: A model always leaves something out. Name one thing the Half-Breath Test leaves out about real lungs.
items.a: Any one of these. In real lungs the blood takes oxygen out and puts carbon dioxide in all the time. Real air is a gas and mixes without a spoon. Real breaths vary in size. Some of each breath only fills the airways.
items.why: A strong answer names a real difference and says how it might change the result. A model is useful because it is simple, and honest only when we say what it leaves out.

items.p: Explain why the blood in the Bean Gill collects more beans moving against the water.
items.a: Moving against the water, a blood cup meets fresher and fresher water as it fills. Just before it leaves, it meets a new water cup with 16 beans. So at every stop the water has more beans than the blood, and beans keep crossing.
items.why: A strong answer says that the fullest blood meets the freshest water, so there is a difference at every stop. Moving the same way, the difference is gone after the first stop.

items.p: Draw an insect's air tubes from one spiracle to a muscle cell. Mark where the oxygen dissolves.
items.a: A hole in the body wall leads to a wide tube. The tube branches into finer and finer tubes. The finest tip touches the muscle cell and holds a little liquid. The oxygen dissolves in that liquid and diffuses into the cell.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the tubes getting finer, ending at the cell itself, with no blood vessel in between.
items.art: A blank outline of a section of an insect's side, with a small oval opening at the edge and a muscle cell drawn deep inside.

items.p: Are your breaths separate things, one after another?

views.says: Yes. Each breath has a start and an end. I can count them: one, two, three.
No. The air in my lungs is a mixture of many breaths. Part of each breath stays in and joins the next.
Counting breaths tells me how ill a child is. Whatever happens to the air inside, the count is real and useful.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give one reason from this lesson. Then say one thing that is right in another view.
items.a: Any view with a reason from the unit. For example: in the Half-Breath Test the water never came from one pour only, so the air inside is shared between breaths. But the movements of the chest can still be counted.
items.why: Each view has something right. The movements of breathing are separate, and the air inside is mixed. A strong answer says which of the two it is talking about.

items.p: A bidi seller says a few puffs do no harm. Use what you know about the alveoli to answer him.
items.a: Alveoli have walls far thinner than a hair, and oxygen must pass through them. Smoke damages these walls and coats the tubes with tar. With time, less oxygen reaches the blood, and breathing diseases follow.
items.why: A strong answer uses the thin wall of the alveolus and says what damage does to the oxygen reaching the blood.

items.p: A slow deep breath changes more of the air in your lungs than a quiet breath. Using the idea of residual air, say what a deep breath cannot do.
items.a: It cannot empty the lungs. About a litre of air always stays in them, even after the hardest breath out.
items.why: A strong answer keeps the idea that the lungs never empty, even in the deepest breath.

quiz.p: Which two systems meet in the alveoli?
quiz.why: The respiratory system brings air to the alveoli. The circulatory system brings blood to the capillaries wrapped round them.

quiz.p: Why can you never breathe out all your air?
opts: Some air always stays in the lungs
The heart is in the way
quiz.why: The chest cannot squeeze the lungs flat. About a litre stays in an adult's lungs after the hardest breath out.

quiz.p: A tumbler loses half its dark water with each 'breath'. When is all the first water gone?
quiz.why: Each breath leaves half of what was there: a half, a quarter, an eighth, and so on. The amount gets too small to see, but halving never reaches zero.

quiz.p: What holds the thin plates of a gill apart?
quiz.why: The plates float free in water. This is why they cling together when a fish is lifted into air.

quiz.p: Blood and water flow the same way past each other. How much oxygen can the blood collect at most?
quiz.why: Oxygen crosses until blood and water hold equal amounts, and then it stops. Flowing opposite ways, the blood can collect far more.

quiz.p: In which animal does blood go from the breathing organ straight on to the body?
quiz.why: A fish has single circulation. Blood leaves the gills and goes on to the body without returning to the heart first.

quiz.p: Why does your right ventricle push more gently than your left?
opts: Lung capillaries have very thin walls
It rests on every second beat
quiz.why: The walls between air and blood in the lungs are extremely thin, so the blood there is kept at low pressure. All of the blood still passes through the lungs.

quiz.p: Where does the haemolymph of a grasshopper flow?
opts: Through the body spaces, round the organs
quiz.why: A grasshopper has an open circulatory system. The tube heart pumps haemolymph out into the spaces of the body.

quiz.p: What shares the work of breathing with a frog's lungs?
quiz.why: A frog's skin is thin, wet and full of capillaries, and a large share of the oxygen crosses there. Frogs have no diaphragm.

quiz.p: What do a bird's air sacs do?
opts: Push air one way through the lungs
Take up most of the oxygen
quiz.why: The air sacs are bellows. Oxygen is taken up in the stiff lungs, and the sacs keep air moving through them in one direction.

quiz.p: In the Squirt Test, what gave the water its push back after the cotton wool?
quiz.why: The water lost its push in the plug. Only a second squeeze sent it far again. In your body, the left ventricle gives that second push.

quiz.p: A doctor says: 'This vessel has thin walls and valves, and it carries blood back to the heart.' What is it?
quiz.why: Veins carry blood back to the heart, and their valves stop it flowing backwards. Arteries, such as the aorta, carry blood away from the heart.

quiz.p: Which is the biggest artery, leaving the left ventricle?
quiz.why: The aorta sends blood to the whole body. The venae cavae are veins that bring blood back. The trachea is not a blood vessel but a tube for air.

quiz.p: A grandfather has a heavy chest, pain spreading to his left arm, and sweating. What should the family do?
opts: Take him to a doctor or hospital at once
quiz.why: These can be signs of a heart attack. Part of his heart muscle may be getting no oxygen, and every minute matters. A heavy meal or sleep wastes time.

quiz.p: Why is smoking bidi bad for the lungs?
opts: The smoke damages the thin walls of the alveoli, so less oxygen crosses into the blood
The smoke makes the lungs grow bigger
The smoke only makes the nose dirty
quiz.why: Alveoli have very thin walls that are easily harmed. Damaged alveoli pass less oxygen to the blood, and breathing diseases follow.

quiz.p: Which set of habits helps keep the heart healthy?
opts: Walking daily, yoga and less fried food
Sitting all day and eating more fried food
quiz.why: Exercise strengthens the heart, yoga and slow breathing calm the body, and less greasy food keeps the arteries clearer. Smoking harms the lungs and the blood vessels.

quiz.p: Air goes from the nose, down the throat, and through a part with the vocal cords on its way to the trachea. What is it?
quiz.why: The larynx is the voice box. The alveoli are the tiny air sacs at the end of the path, and the diaphragm is the muscle under the lungs.

quiz.p: A tulsi plant sits in a dark cupboard overnight. Which gas does it take in?
opts: Neither, because plants do not breathe
quiz.why: Plant cells need oxygen day and night, like ours. In the dark, the leaves cannot make food from light, so the plant gives out carbon dioxide and no extra oxygen.
